Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 36, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

(Yā-Sīn) It is permissible for these to be disjoined letters (ḥurūf muqaṭṭa'ah) like (Alif-Lām-Mīm) and (Ṭā-Hā), and it is also permissible for them to be disjoined letters that happen to coincide with a proper name; therefore among his names ﷺ are Yā-Sīn and Ṭā-Hā. There is no objection to a name consisting of two letters, or even of a single letter, such as (Nūn) in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe﴾ [al-Qalam: 1], and it has been made a proper name for our master Dhu'l-Nūn, peace be upon him. Likewise (Qāf) has become the name of the well-known mountain. So: these are disjoined letters, which can be transferred to the status of proper names and be used as names.

We have often spoken about the disjoined letters at the beginnings of the surahs, and whenever disjoined letters come before us we must speak of the meanings they may bear. What is firmly fixed in the mind is that a letter has a name and a named referent (musammā). The name of the letter is known only to the learner, whereas the referent of the letter is known to both the learner and the unlettered. The unlettered person, for example, knows the verb (akala, "he ate") and says "akaltu" ("I ate"), but he cannot spell out its letters, because he knows only the referents of the letters. The learner, however, knows the name of the letter and says: "alif fatḥah", "kāf fatḥah", and "lām fatḥah". How then did Muḥammad ﷺ come to know the names of these letters and pronounce them, when he was the unlettered one who could neither read nor write? The answer: he was taught and made to know by his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

The Qur'an came as a miracle, challenging the people in that wherein they excelled, and the Arabs were a people of eloquence and expression. It suffices that they used to hold exhibitions and markets for the word, just as we today hold exhibitions for distinguished crafts; and well known among the Arabs were the market of ʿUkāẓ, the market of al-Mirbad and al-Majannah, etc.

Their concern with the word and style went so far that they would hang the famous poems they had on the Kaʿbah, and these poems were called "al-Muʿallaqāt" (the Suspended Odes), and they are the most famous of what is known of pre-Islamic poetry.

That the Qur'an challenges them is a testimony to their superiority, for one does not challenge the weak but the strong, as we see now, for example, in the breaking of a record in some field.

The Qur'an's challenge to the Arabs in eloquence and rhetoric is like the challenge of our master Mūsā to the magicians, and the challenge of our master ʿĪsā to the physicians. So: this is an established practice among all nations, in which the Truth, glory be to Him, challenges them in that wherein they excelled. Likewise the noble Qur'an came in the language of the Arabs, their letters and their words which they pronounce, and yet they were unable to produce its like. Why, although the material of speech is one?

They said: Because the one speaking the Qur'an is the Truth, glory be to Him.

We have clarified this matter with an example — and to God belongs the highest likeness — we said: If you wish to test a group of weavers to see which of them is the most skilled, you must not give one of them silk, another cotton, and another wool, because the raw material differs; rather you give all of them one material, and then you look at the weaving of each of them. Likewise the Qur'an and the language of the Arabs: the material is one, but the speaker here is the Arabs, and the speaker here is the Truth, glory be to Him.

When you contemplate the letters of Arabic you find them to be twenty-eight letters, and the disjoined letters in the Qur'an are fourteen, so they are half of the Arabic letters. The Imam Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, may God have mercy on him, has an astonishing table which arranges these letters and shows that they were placed thus for a wisdom, and were placed with measure and calculation. These fourteen letters are divided as follows:

The total of the letters of the language is twenty-eight letters. The first nine, beginning from the alif up to the dhāl, the disjoined letters took from them only two letters: the alif and the ḥā', and left seven of them. As for the last nine letters, beginning from the fā', the disjoined letters took from them seven letters, namely: the qāf, the kāf, the lām, the mīm, the nūn, the hā', and the yā', and left the fā' and the wāw. So it is, then, the reverse of the first nine.

As for the ten letters in the middle, which begin from the rā' and end with the ghayn, they have another arrangement: the disjoined letters took from them the unpointed letters, namely the rā', the sīn, the ṣād, the ṭā', and the ʿayn, and left from them the zāy, the shīn, the ḍād, the ẓā', and the ghayn.

Likewise, when we contemplate, for example, the letters of the throat, you find that the khā' in the first group was not mentioned among the disjoined letters, and the mīm was mentioned in the last group.

Thus we see that these letters were not placed thus haphazardly or as things happened, but were placed with a measure and an order which has a wisdom and secrets behind it; they were placed with a deliberately intended design. They are like the teeth of a key, and God, glory be to Him, opens with them to whomever He wills. And among His wisdom, exalted is He, is that He did not give all the secrets of these letters to one generation; rather He distributed their bounty across the passage of time, so that no generation receives the words of God without bounty, and so that the Qur'an remains a light illuminating the corners of the world until the Hour is established. Therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 53].

This sīn denoting the future was pronounced by our master, the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said ﴿sanurīhim﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 53], and secrets appeared in his time; and those after him of successive generations pronounced it, and secrets appeared for them; and we shall continue to pronounce it, and its secrets will be manifested to us until the Hour is established, and until the greatest sign appears, which is the Resurrection. So: the bounty of the Qur'an is a continuous bounty that never ceases.

Therefore, when we discussed with some orientalists in San Francisco the matter of inventors and discoverers who served humanity and made it happy through their inventions and discoveries, one of them said: "How strange are the Muslims! Why do these discoverers who made humanity happy not enter Paradise?" We explained to him that indeed they served humanity, but not for the sake of God; for God was not in their minds when they discovered what they discovered; rather, in their minds were fame, glory and remembrance among people, and they obtained what they wanted, and we immortalized their memory and erected statues for them, etc. — so the hadith applies to them: So: those scholars who served humanity and made it happy, while not believing in God, are nothing but servants whom God subjected to serve mankind. They are like the sun, the moon and others, which God subjected to man for his benefit and his advantage; they are nothing but soldiers of God's soldiers serving this letter in ﴿sanurīhim﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 53], so that it continues to give through the passage of time and in all the future.

The likeness of these scholars who do not believe in God is like the likeness of a servant of yours to whom you said: "Carry this stone, for example," and he said to you: "It is heavy upon me; I cannot bear to carry it." If you said to him: "Seek help from someone who will carry it with you," he might say: "I cannot find anyone." But if you said to him: "Carry it, and you will find beneath it a treasure which is yours," then he would carry it alone. In that case, does he carry it out of respect for your command, or does he carry it out of desire for the treasure?

Likewise, when the sciences advanced, they discovered that wine harms the liver, so many abstained from drinking it out of fear of its harm, after they had come to know the cause. As for the believer, he abstains from it before he knows this truth; he abstains because his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, forbade him to drink it, so he ceases out of trust in the wisdom of his Lord and out of respect for His command, even if he does not know the cause.

And because Surah Yā-Sīn — it is established in a hadith that it is the heart of the Qur'an — it is necessary that we begin with the seeking of refuge and the basmalah before it, as we began them in the surahs before it. The Truth, glory be to Him, who sent down the Qur'an as a miracle and a book of guidance upon our master, the Messenger of God, to correct the movement of life for the believers in it, said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Naḥl: 98].

We have said previously that the reason for this command from on high is that Satan, when he disobeyed his Lord in prostrating to Adam, and the dialogue took place between him and his Lord, said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Ṣād: 82], meaning: so that Adam and his descendants will not be distinguished from me in disobedience, ﴿except for Your chosen servants among them﴾ [Ṣād: 83]. So his saying ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Ṣād: 82] means: to make them take a path other than the path which God laid down for them; and the path which God laid down for them is the straight path, of which He said: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'rāf: 16].

Yes, because Satan does not come to the tavern nor to places of gambling and sin; rather he confronts the people of obedience to spoil their obedience. The straight path here is the method of God which He set down to make mankind happy. So Iblīs, instead of waiting until the method of God is carried out in the movement of the limbs, in obedience and disobedience, comes to the foundation from which those limbs take the method of movement; so when you recite the Qur'an, he comes to spoil the recitation for you.

Therefore your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, teaches you the seeking of refuge: first, to cut off this path from Satan, for he will not wait for you until you recite, and until you bring the fruit of this recitation into the movement of life; rather he comes to the Qur'an itself and spoils it for you from the beginning. So if you wish to overcome him, seek refuge in God from him.

When you seek refuge in God from him, you take refuge in a strong pillar and a protecting shield, through which nothing of Satan's whispering, his prodding and his nudging can penetrate you. Therefore Satan was aware when he said: ﴿except for Your chosen servants among them﴾ [Ṣād: 83], for they are those who shelter from him in the sanctuary of their Lord and their Creator.

As for the words of the Exalted ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾: the Truth, glory be to Him, created man and made him the lord of this universe, and subjected everything to him; and among what He subjected to him, He subjected his parts to his will. So He subjected, for example, his tongue to his will: if he is a believer, he says "God is one"; and if he is otherwise, he says "God is the third of three." Likewise He subjected the eye to him, to look at what is permitted and at what is forbidden; likewise the foot. So all your limbs God has subjected to you: if you desire obedience from them, they obey; if you desire disobedience from them, they disobey. The will is what dictates what you desire, and the limbs cannot do anything but execute obedience or disobedience, because they are subjected.

We have previously given an example of this: the supreme commander of an army, when he sends, for example, a subordinate commander at the head of a battalion on some mission, the battalion must obey the order of this immediate commander with blind obedience, even if these orders are not in their favour; and they have no right to object to him. Then, when they return to the supreme commander, they complain to him about what their immediate commander did. Likewise is the obedience of the limbs to the will of man in this world.

As for the Hereafter, this leadership over his limbs will be taken from him, and his limbs will testify against their owner before the Supreme Truth, glory be to Him; for in the Hereafter there is no authority for anyone but God: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today? To God, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghāfir: 16].

He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The day when their tongues and their hands and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nūr: 24].

And He said: ﴿And they will say to their skins: "Why did you testify against us?" They will say: "God has made us speak, who made everything speak"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 21].

So when you want an action, this action first requires of you an intellectual, thinking power which plans it; then it requires strength in the limbs to act. Who created for you the thinking mind? And who supplied your limbs with strength and effective energy? Do they obey you and do your desired action by a self-generated power within them, or by God's decree for them?

Therefore it is necessary that you approach every act — in thought, planning, execution and deed — by saying "In the name of God." When you say it, it is as though you are saying to the limbs: "I do not demand from you by my own strength, but from the inner power of 'In the name of God.' By the name of God I act, not by myself."

As evidence: if God, exalted is He, willed to strip man of self-initiated movement, self-initiated energy and thought, the limbs would be paralysed and thinking would be paralysed. So approach all your deeds with "In the name of God," who helps you in them.

Then in actions you need wisdom, power, knowledge, etc. So who gathers all these attributes? It is God. So say: "In the name of God," who gathers all the attributes of perfection in their entirety, who supplies His creation with them: He, glory be to Him, is the Knowing who supplies you with knowledge, the Powerful who supplies you with power, the Wise who supplies you with wisdom, the Mighty who supplies you with might, the Subduer who supplies you with subjugation, etc.

Do we not hear the judge say, when he sits to pass judgement: "In the name of the people" — meaning: he does not judge by his own essence, but by the power of the people. Likewise the believer says "In the name of God" at every act, meaning: O limbs, obey me from the inner core of your obedience to God.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, describes Himself with His saying ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 1], because the Truth, glory be to Him, created creation with freedom of choice, so among them were the believer and the disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient; and perhaps man forgets the method of God, so minor sins and even major sins proceed from him. How then can he approach his deed with "In the name of God"? And how can he seek help from Him, glory be to Him, when he has disobeyed Him?

Therefore his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, says to him: Do not be shy to say "In the name of God," for I am the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful; I forgive you and overlook what has happened from you, and I will not abandon you. So: take courage and do not leave off seeking help by My name, whatever sins you have committed, and rely in that upon the fact that I am the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It has been related that al-Aṣmaʿī heard a man saying, while circumambulating the Kaʿbah: "O God, I am disobeying You, and I am ashamed to ask You; but from whom should I ask, when there is nothing in existence except You?" So al-Aṣmaʿī said to him: "O man, your Lord has answered you because of the goodness of your asking of Him."

When the Truth, glory be to Him, enumerates His blessings upon His servants, He says: ﴿And if you were to count the blessings of God, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 34]. Indeed, because counting a thing is the presumption of enumerating it; and despite the advance of the sciences and the specialisation of universities and institutes for statistics, no one has undertaken to count the blessings of God, because they cannot be counted; rather, within a single blessing lies hidden what cannot be enumerated of blessings. Therefore He, glory be to Him, did not say: "If you count the blessings of God," but "the blessing of God," for within a single blessing is concealed what cannot be grasped of blessings.

We notice in this verse that it occurs in two places, but each of them has a concluding phrase: the first: ﴿And if you were to count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it; indeed, man is surely a wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 34]; and the other: ﴿And if you were to count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it; indeed, God is surely Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Naḥl: 18].

It is as though the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to us: you, O human being, upon whom blessing has been bestowed, respond to the blessings of God with wrongdoing and ingratitude; but your Lord, the Bestower, glory be to Him, responds to your wrongdoing and your ingratitude toward His blessings by continuing the blessings, because He is Forgiving and Merciful.

And the scholars have opinions about (Yā-Sīn). They said: the yā' is for the vocative, and the sīn is one of his names, ﷺ; because it is the habit of the Arabs to drop some letters of a word and keep the letter that is distinctive and strong in its resonance. For example, in the word insān (human being), the sīn is the strongest letter in it; therefore the saying of the Prophet ﷺ came: and the intended meaning is: "shāhidan" (as a witness).

Among that is the saying of the poet:

O Fāṭim, gently, with some of this coquetry, even if you have resolved to cut me off, then be gracious.

And the intended meaning is: Fāṭimah.

In our daily speech we also abbreviate some letters: when we call, for example, "yā Aḥmad", some of us do not pronounce the dāl, especially in the dialect of the people of Damietta. So: dropping some letters and keeping others that have a strong resonance is a matter that occurs in the language of the Arabs.

Others said: rather, his name ﷺ is (Yā-Sīn), and the vocative yā' has been dropped, addressed to Muḥammad ﷺ.

The Truth, glory be to Him, taught man all the names: that is, He taught him the word required for him in address; then, when man speaks and addresses others, he agrees upon and settles on other names, so man, for example, now knows (the television) and becomes familiar with this name. Did God teach Adam the name "television"? No; rather man agreed upon it with what God taught him.

So the meaning: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], that is: those suitable for his address now in the primitive environment; and it is incumbent upon him to develop his language, so that he gives this thing such-and-such a name and that thing such-and-such a name.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 36, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

We know that letters are of two kinds. The first kind is letters of structure (huruf mabnā), whose function is to build the word, without having any meaning beyond that. For example, we say: kataba (he wrote). The kāf, the tā' and the bā' are letters from which this word is built, without giving any meaning beyond the meaning of this verb which the letters have formed.

The second kind is letters of meaning (huruf ma'nā), where the letter has a meaning that it indicates in itself, as when we say: katabtu (I wrote). This final tā' carries a meaning other than the meaning of writing, because it indicates the doer who is the speaker. If it comes with a fatḥah, it indicates the addressed doer (the one addressed), and if it comes with a kasrah, it indicates the feminine, and so on.

We have also said that the name of a letter may coincide with a designation for something. The sīn, for example, is the name of a well-known river, and the ʿayn is a letter of the alphabet, but many things have been named by it: the ʿayn (eye) that sees, the spring of water (ʿayn al-māʾ), the ʿayn meaning a spy, and the ʿayn meaning a precious item of wealth, of gold or silver.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 2], this wāw is called the wāw of oath (wāw al-qasam), and what it enters upon is like an oath. But does the speaker, in seeking from the addressee what he wants, use an oath or evidence? He uses evidence, though an oath may come in which there is an indication of the intended aim. For example, your friend says to you: "My brother, you have not valued me, because I passed through a crisis and you did not stand by me." So you say to him: "By the life of the cheque that I wrote to you on such-and-such day, and by the life of the gift that you took on such-and-such day," swearing to him by the evidence of your truthfulness.

Likewise here, the Truth, blessed and exalted, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): You are a messenger, and I swear by the Qur'an, because it is evidence that you are a truthful messenger.

The word Qur'ān is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of qaraʾa. You say qara'tu qirāʾatan and qur'ānan, and there is no doubt that an increase in structure indicates an increase in meaning. So we said qur'ānan to distinguish the reading of the Qur'an from the reading of other things. It also indicates that it is a book that is read. Another time He calls it the Book, because it is written. So the Qur'an is read from the breasts and written in the lines.

Another time He calls it the Reminder (al-dhikr), because it reminds us of the covenant of the first natural disposition (fiṭrah), about which Allah said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172].

This reminder of the first covenant is considered a mercy from Allah to us. It is part of Allah's mercy to us that He reminds us when we forget or become heedless. From the time Adam was created until now, the Truth, blessed and exalted, has been reminding His servants. Just as a father teaches his child the movements of life, he first teaches him the movements of this religion. This teaching and reminding must continue and follow on from generation to generation, because human nature contains heedlessness and forgetfulness, and disobedience occurs from him.

Therefore, those who said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22] are lying in this statement, because Adam and his community were at the beginning upon guidance. So why did you not follow them? Thus: you followed the misguided fathers, not the guided ones.

Likewise, when you consider the matter of the collection of the Qur'an, you find that those who collected the Qur'an were careful, before recording a verse, that it be first written on parchment (qirṭās) or on the scraps and bones on which the Qur'an was first recorded. Then two of the reciters would bear witness to its correctness. Why? They said: because parchment has no whim, so it does not alter what is written on it, whereas the human who memorises is prone to error, forgetfulness and heedlessness. So there must be another with him to remind him, in accordance with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other can remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

The Qur'an, Allah described it as wisdom (ḥikmah), which is placing a thing in its correct place so that it fulfils its function. Every religious meaning is taken from sensible things that precede religion. For example, a horse is ridden by a person so that it carries him to his aims. If your aim in riding the horse is to take a stroll among the fields, it moves you at a slow pace like the pace of a hantour carriage, for example, and if you want to cover a distance with it, it runs you like the wind.

Therefore they made for the horse a bit (lijām) that is placed in its jaw to restrain its speed and to control it. This bit is called al-ḥakamah, and from it comes ḥikmah, which restrains the rush of desires so that they do not wander off and so that matters are placed in their proper place. A human has a desire that inclines him and turns his movement away from the right path, so the Qur'an brings the clear truth that straightens this inclination and corrects it. The Qur'an is in reality ḥakīm (wise), because it was made firm (muḥkam) by the Supreme Wise One, the Exalted. So: the Qur'an is speech from the Wise, and for humans it is like the ḥakamah for the horse.

Because of its wisdom, the Qur'an has been singled out for certain things. Handling the Qur'an is not like handling other books. An ordinary book, I may handle at any time and in any state, whether I am junub or in a state of minor impurity. But the Qur'an is not touched except by one who is pure, because with the Qur'an you approach a sacred thing that has its own distinctiveness. So beware of handling it while you are impure, as the Truth, Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-protected, which none touches except the purified﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 77–79].

Thus the Truth, Glorified, has given you these psychological controls so that you know that you are approaching a book that has a distinction above all other books.

Likewise, the Qur'an has a distinctiveness in its letters. The letters are what form the words, and they are sound-articulations, each of which has a place (makhraj) in the organs of speech. For example, the letters that come out from the cavity of the throat and the chest are:

Hamzah, hāʾ, then ʿayn and ḥāʾ, two unaspirated ones, then ghayn and fāʾ.

If we leave the region of the throat, we find the tongue letters, which are pronounced from the tongue, beginning with (its root, lughlughah) then its middle, then its tip. For example, the qāf comes out from the far end of the tongue, the shīn and jīm from its middle, and the ḍād, lām and rāʾ from its tip. Likewise there are letters that come out from the lips: the fāʾ from the inner part of the lower lip, the bāʾ from the inner part of both lips together, and the wāw is pronounced with the participation of both lips.

In order to recite the Qur'an correctly, we must adhere to these phonetic points of articulation, unlike the recitation of any other book, for which this condition is not required. Therefore we say: the perfection of the Qur'an is not transgressed, since it has a specific manner and a precise melody, which must be observed.

For example, if you are speaking in an ordinary sermon and say: "O gentlemen, peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings, and after: so-and-so has summoned me to meet him in such-and-such a place..." If you were to utter this speech in the melody and manner of the Qur'an, it would be something unacceptable (bāyikh, vulgar). But if this melody is in the Qur'an, it comes beautiful and harmonious.

So: the perfection of the Qur'an is not transgressed even in its pronunciation, because this is something specific to it alone, apart from other speech. If you extend the distinctive features of the Qur'an to other speech, it comes out weak and rejected, not accepted.

I recall, when we were young, that they used to advise us to read books of literature, such as the books of al-Manfalūṭī, like "al-ʿIbarāt" or "al-Naẓarāt," to learn the beautiful style in his composition. Indeed, our style would improve and advance by reading books of literature, and we would acquire new expressions from them. But if you come to a Qur'an memoriser who has perfected it according to the ten readings or the fourteen, and you read to him a word or an article, you will find that his style is not affected by the Qur'an. Why? Because the perfection of the Qur'anic style is not transgressed.

So: we understand that the wisdom of the Qur'an comes from this distinctiveness: in its letters there is wisdom, in its words there is wisdom, and in its arrangement, its recitation, and in its style, which cannot be matched and cannot be transferred to anything else.

Then the Truth, Glorified, says:
﴿Indeed, you are of the messengers﴾.

The Qur'an's oath, the "wa" (the particle of oath, known as wāw al-qasam) and what it introduces is like an oath. But does the speaker, when seeking what he wants from the listener, bring an oath or evidence? He brings evidence, though an oath may also come with it, indicating the intended purpose. For example, your friend says to you: "Brother, you did not appreciate me, because I went through a crisis and you did not stand by my side," so you say to him: "By the life of the cheque I wrote to you on such-and-such day, and by the life of the gift you received on such-and-such day," swearing to him by evidence of your truthfulness.

Likewise here, the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): You are a messenger, and I swear by the Qur'an, because it is evidence that you are a truthful messenger.

The word "Qur'an" is a verbal noun of qara'a. You say qara'tu qirā'atan and qur'ānan. The increase in the form (al-mabnā) necessarily indicates an increase in meaning (al-ma'nā). So we say qur'ān to distinguish the recitation of the Qur'an from the recitation of other things. It also indicates that it is a book that is recited. Another name for it is "the Book" because it is written. The Qur'an, then, is recited from the chests (ṣudūr) and written on the lines (suṭūr).

Another name for it is "the Reminder" (al-dhikr), because it reminds us of the covenant of the primordial nature (fiṭrah), concerning which Allah said:

﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." (This), lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware."﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]...

And Allah described the Qur'an as "wise" (ḥakīm). Wisdom (ḥikmah) is placing a thing in its rightful place so that it fulfils its function. All religious meanings are derived from sensible things that precede religion. For example, a horse is ridden by a person so that it may carry him to his aims. If your aim in riding the horse is to take a leisurely trip through the fields, it moves you slowly, like a carriage (ḥanṭūr) for instance; and if you want to cover the distance, it runs with you like the wind. For this reason they made a bit (lijām) for the horse, placed in its jaw to restrain its speed and control it. This bit is called al-ḥakamah, and from it comes ḥikmah, which restrains the bridles of desires so that they do not stray, and places matters in their proper place. Man has a desire that inclines him and, by its movement, deviates him from the right path, so the Qur'an brings the clear truth that straightens this inclination and corrects it. The Qur'an is, in reality, wise, because it is made firm (muḥkam) by the Supreme Wise One, may He be glorified. Thus, the Qur'an is speech from the Wise, and in relation to man it is like the bit to the horse.

Because of the wisdom of the Qur'an, it is distinguished by certain things. Handling the Qur'an is not like handling other books. An ordinary book I may handle at any time and in any state, whether I am in a state of major impurity (junub) or minor impurity (muḥdith). But the Qur'an is touched only by one who is pure, because when you approach the Qur'an you are approaching something sacred that has its own distinction. So beware of handling it while you are impure, as the True One, may He be glorified, said: ﴿Indeed, it is an honourable Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77-79].

Thus Allah has made for you these psychological safeguards so that you know you are approaching a book that has a distinction over all other books...

So we understand that the wisdom of the Qur'an comes from this distinction: there is wisdom in its letters, wisdom in its words, and in its arrangement (naẓm), its recitation (tartīl), and in its style, which is unmatched and cannot be transferred to anything else.

This is the answer to the oath. Allah, glory be to Him, responds to the disbelievers of Makkah and swears to them: "Indeed, you, O Muhammad, are among the messengers."

When a speaker sees that the addressee is free of any doubt about the matter he is speaking of, he delivers his words naturally, without emphasis. But if the addressee is doubtful about the words or denies them, the speaker reinforces his speech with an emphasis that suits the doubt or the denial.

Therefore Allah, glory be to Him, here reinforces His speech with more than one emphasis: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. He uses the emphasis of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) and the lam of emphasis, and before that the oath, because the disbelievers deny his prophethood, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The degree of emphasis in speech matches the degree of denial.

Consider His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them both, so We strengthened them with a third, and they said, "Indeed, we are messengers to you."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14]. The result was denial: ﴿They said, "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 15].

Therefore they reinforce their own statement with more than one emphasis: ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 16].

We have said that this verse came as evidence and proof in the form of an oath, as if Allah were saying: whoever reads the Qur'an must believe that you, O Muhammad, are a messenger sent by Allah. Why? Because they were a people of speech and refinement of language. No nation has existed, even among contemporary nations, that holds exhibitions for the word. As for the Arabs in their pre-Islamic age (jahiliyyah), they established markets and fairs for the word, in which orators and poets competed every year at al-Mirbad, 'Ukaz, Dhu al-Majaz and others.

Their concern with the word reached the point that they hung their finest odes on the curtains of the Ka'bah. Since the Arabs were a people of speech, they should have received the Qur'an with this faculty, and its inimitability should not have been hidden from them. But they denied it and said: "It is magic," and said: "It is poetry," and said: "It is fabrication." When their stratagems failed them and they gained nothing from that, they said:

﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 31]. That is, the Qur'an has no flaw, except that it is sent down upon Muhammad; this is its defect in their eyes, because their eloquent faculty cannot stand before the Qur'an or deny it.

Therefore, even while in their disbelief, they loved to hear the Qur'an. One of them would conceal himself and go to listen to the Qur'an from the Messenger of Allah at night... So when one of them heard the Qur'an from the Messenger of Allah and returned to his people, they would say: "So-and-so has returned in a state other than the one in which he went."

Al-Sirat (the path) has another meaning on the Day of Resurrection: it is the bridge laid over the back of Hell (Jahannam), which the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, all cross. How a person crosses it differs according to his deeds in this world. One crosses it like a lightning flash, though it is sharper than the edge of a sword and finer than a hair. Another crosses it like the fastest racehorse. Another crosses it crawling, and another falls into Hell, may God protect us.

When you cross the sirat, you will have no staff with which to keep your balance, like a circus tightrope walker, for what balances your movement on the sirat is the Qur'an, which you held fast to in this world. So when the believer crosses the sirat, his balance comes not from beneath him but from above, from the direction of the Qur'an. He is like the suspension bridges that are not supported by anything underneath, but are held taut from above by what grips them and preserves their balance. Such is the condition of the believer on the sirat.

In its general sense, the sirat is the straight path that brings you to your goal by the shortest and easiest distance. But the Qur'anic expression ﴿upon a straight path﴾ [Ya-Sin: 4] contains an indication that the sirat has a function: that it delivers you to the intended goal. The sirat is therefore at your service.

Similarly, God's saying ﴿upon guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. Some understand that guidance entails obligations and the restriction of movement, and that there is hardship and difficulty in guidance. But the wording of the verse means the opposite. The meaning of ﴿upon guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] is that you ride upon guidance, as though it were a mount that carries you to your glorious goal. It carries you; you do not carry it.

As for describing the sirat as straight, we learned in geometry that a straight line is the shortest distance between two points. When you want, for example, to move from one place to another, "min" (from) marks the starting point and "ila" (to) marks the goal you want. As long as you are concerned only with the beginning and the end, ease requires that you take the shortest and most direct route, which is the straight line. For every bend in the road or turn along the way forms a triangle of two sides, with the straight road being the third side.

It is known that the sum of any two sides of a triangle is longer than the third. Therefore the road becomes long for you. That is why the Qur'an speaks to us of the straight path, and of the even way (sawa' al-sabil), meaning that the right side is equal to the left side.

But why was the way of the believers a straight path? Because God Most High is the One who legislated it as the method for His creation, and because it is sent down from God.

Whenever you hear the word tanzil (revelation, "sending down"), know that it comes from the direction of what is above, even if the thing sent down is within the depths of the earth; for in reality it came from on high, as in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for mankind﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]... And His saying: ﴿the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. Here He, glorified is He, mentions the attribute of might and the attribute of mercy, because the tanzil is from the highest methodology, which restricts the movement of the human being: "do this" and "do not do that," while you are free to obey or disobey. The Truth who legislated this methodology for you desires good for you, since He, glorified is He, gains nothing from your obedience and is not harmed by your disobedience.

So: you are the object of this matter, for Allah, exalted is He, is Mighty above His creation and Merciful toward them. When you look at the disobedient one who opposes the methodology of Allah, Allah is Mighty, able to take vengeance; no one can take you out of the grip of the Exalted. And when you look at the obedient one, Allah is Merciful.

The reason for the sending down:

﴿That you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾...

... And His saying: ﴿So they are heedless﴾. Heedlessness (al-ghafla) is that a thing occurs to your mind, and then your heart does not become attached to it, until it enters the level of forgetting, so you do not recall it except when someone comes who alerts you to it and reminds you of it. Forgetting is not the function of the heart; rather, the function belongs to the intellect (al-'aql) and the memory (al-dhakira). For if the heart were attached to a thing, then whenever heedlessness arose regarding it, the heart would attach itself to that which closes the gap, so it would remain in the memory and you would not be heedless of it.

Al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 36, verse 7:

The Truthful One, glory be to Him and exalted is He, inscribed from eternity everything that will occur from those who will receive any religious call, whether they believe in it or disbelieve. Yet He, glory be to Him, left choice to people. His being exalted would record what will happen from people, and then the event comes from them in accordance with what He recorded. This means that what He said of old is true.

The Qur'an says once ﴿حَقَّ الْقَوْلُ﴾ (the Word has become due) [Ya-Sin: 7], once ﴿سَبَقَ عَلَيْهِ الْقَوْلُ﴾ (the Word has preceded against him) [Hud: 40], and once ﴿وَقَعَ الْقَوْلُ﴾ (the Word has come to pass) [An-Naml: 82].

All of them indicate that what has preceded in the knowledge of God, concerning the one who chooses to be guided or to go astray, is recorded with Him, exalted is He, and it is true as God has reported it. Had the servant not been free to choose, we would say that God compelled him to what He willed, but he is a chooser.

The Truthful One, exalted is He, has absolute power and absolute knowledge. Because of His knowledge of what will be, He recorded and wrote...

In this verse, the Truth, glorified is He, gives us a depiction of the state of these disbelievers who turn away from following the Truth. He says: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, and they reach to the chins, so they are made to hold their heads up﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8]. Al-aghlal (the shackles): its singular is ghull, which is the iron ring that holds the hand and binds it under the chin. When the hand is bound under the chin, the head is raised upward, and consequently the level of the gaze rises upward, so a person can barely see his path and cannot find the place of his foot.

This image is also clear in the meaning of the word ﴿muqmahun﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8]. Al-muqmah is derived from qammah camels (qimah al-ibil), which is that when they go to drink water, they scoop it up, then raise their heads upward.

Some of them said: This is an image that the Truth, glorified is He, drew for one who chains his hand from giving charity and from spending. Likewise, his hand will be chained to his neck on the Day of Resurrection, such that this shackle affects his path upon which he built the movement of his life. The Truth, glorified is He, always balances between what the one deserving of recompense did and the recompense, for the recompense is of the same kind as the deed.

An example of this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah﴾ [At-Tawbah: 34]. This is the deed; so what is the recompense? ﴿Give them tidings of a painful punishment, on the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads, their sides, and their backs will be branded with it: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard"﴾ [At-Tawbah: 34–35].

These are three places on the human body: the foreheads (al-jibah), the sides (al-junub), and the backs (al-zuhur). They came in this order to match exactly what the owner of wealth did when he hoarded his money and grudged it to the poor. The poor man would come to him, and he would turn his forehead away from him, give him his side, then turn his back to him and walk away. So their punishment came in proportion to what they had done.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier...﴾.

Is the meaning of this that God Most High helps them and assists them in disbelief? They said: Yes, because when My servant calls upon Me and he disdains My call and does not turn to Me in servitude to Me, I assist him in his disbelief, for I am a Lord who is independent of him. So if he loves disbelief and is infatuated with it, and there is no longer hope of his guidance, I seal his heart, so that faith does not enter it and disbelief does not leave it. Therefore, whoever wrongs you and turns away from you, then assist him in that, and do not remind him of yourself.

So: no one disbelieves against the will of God; rather, he disbelieves by means of the choice that God has placed in him. And since He, glory be to Him, is Lord and is the Creator of the servants, it is incumbent upon Him, glory be to Him, to assist them, each according to what he wills. So whoever wills faith and loves it, He assists him in faith; and whoever wills disbelief and is infatuated with it, He likewise assists him in it and supports him.

Therefore God sealed the hearts of the disbelievers, and here He says: ﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier﴾, meaning: in front of them a obstructing and preventing barrier, and behind them a barrier.

This is a physical barrier, outside the constitution of the human being. ﴿And We have covered them, so they do not see﴾, meaning: We placed upon their sight a veil and a covering, so they are blocked from the truth for several reasons. First: within their own selves. We covered their sight so they do not see and are not guided, because they, in their own selves, have not remembered the primordial covenant of the fitrah upon which God created people.

As for what is outside of them, it lies in the path to which they paid no attention, neither in what is before them nor in what is behind them, because there is a barrier that prevents them. Had they considered what awaits them, they would have refrained from their error; and had they reflected on what befell the deniers who came before them, and what the punishment of God struck them with, they would have turned back.

But God placed before them a barrier, so they do not know what awaits them, and behind them a barrier, so they do not reflect on what befell their predecessors, of whom God said:

﴿So each one We seized for his sin; among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those seized by the Blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40].

If you say: God Most High placed a barrier that prevents them from the front, and a barrier that prevents them from the back; what if they walk to the side, to the right or to the left? They said: If they walked and turned to the left, for example, then the left would become front for them, and the right would become behind; so they are surrounded by barriers, such that there is no hope for them of returning to the path of truth and to rightness.

It is also valid that the meaning is: ﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier﴾, that is: an obstruction preventing them from contemplating and looking at the rational proofs set up before them so that they might believe; and ﴿behind them a barrier﴾ prevents them, so they do not arrive at the innate faith deposited within them.

Equally so for them, not for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has only the duty of conveying the message. Once he has conveyed it to them, his mission is complete. It is as if Allah were saying to him: "Be at peace and do not grieve. Whether you warn them or not makes no difference to them. It is by your warning that the proof has been established against them, for they swore in an earlier passage:

﴿And they swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them, they would surely be better guided than any of the (other) nations. But when a warner came to them, it only increased them in aversion.﴾ [Fatir: 42].

Meaning: your warning, O Muhammad, is effective only with the one who remembers God and fears Him, believes in Him, and believes in His power over resurrection and reckoning. This is the one who benefits from the warning and profits from it, unlike the denier who contradicts the fundamental principle. How does he benefit from the warning? The meaning of ﴿ٱتَّبَعَ ٱلذِّكْرَ﴾ [Yasin: 11] is: the Qur'an.

Khashyah (fear with awe): it is fear, but fear accompanied by reverence. You fear God and revere Him, and likewise you hope in Him. As for fear of other than God, it is fear with aversion, because it is fear of tyranny. Therefore, after khashyah comes the attribute of mercy: ﴿وَخشِيَ ٱلرَّحْمـٰنَ﴾ [Yasin: 11]. You fear One who is characterized by tenderness and compassion, and this is more likely to make you love the One you fear and turn you toward Him in kindness, so your fear of Him is mixed with awe, dignity, and hope in Him. Therefore He, glorified be He, said: ﴿وَخشِيَ ٱلرَّحْمـٰنَ﴾ [Yasin: 11], so that you do not flee from the One you fear.

This khashyah is found in the believer ﴿بِٱلْغَيْبِ﴾ [Yasin: 11], meaning: at the time when he is absent from people and alone. He fears God and does not fear people, and he has no need of a watcher, because human surveillance of humans is of no use: you would be appointing over him a watcher of his own kind, and whatever is permissible for the one observed is permissible for the observer, such as deception and other things, even when you place a sudden inspection over the observer, you are not safe from deception.

We have previously given the example of the traffic policeman. Before one of us is permitted to drive a car, he must pass harsh conditions that first guarantee the safety of the car he drives, then enable him to master the art of driving, and he must pass the tests necessary for that. Yet despite all this, some of us abide by the traffic rules and some of us do not. Therefore we station a traffic policeman to monitor and regulate traffic on the streets, and over him there is someone who monitors him.

But when they found that the traffic policeman could be deceptive, taking a bribe from a violator and overlooking another, they invented monitoring devices such as radars, to be more accurate. But who operates these devices? Humans, to whom what applies to others also applies.

So: when the observer is of the same kind as the observed, the process of observation is of no benefit. And if we placed a watcher over each of us, we would need armies of guards.

So: what do we do to govern this whole world?

Muhammad (ﷺ) came, and his message has the features of a complete message. His message is not limited by time or by place. Time and place are what confine events; they are the containers of an event, so if no event exists, there is neither time nor place. Therefore it is not correct to say, regarding God, the Exalted: "where" or "when," because "where" and "when" are created by God.

Although time and place share the quality of being containers for an event, place is a fixed container, meaning stable, while time is a changing container. This is its time, the morning, and this is noon, and we say: this is before such-and-such, and this is after such-and-such.

The Messenger of God came with a message general in time and in place until the Hour is established, and he came with a method for safeguarding the human being throughout the whole world, despite the differences of its environments and natures, and across the ages with their differing eras. So how is this safeguarding and this monitoring achieved? Since Muhammad (ﷺ) came with a method to govern the whole world in time and place, it is not correct that a watcher of his own kind be placed over each individual, nor even from the angels. Rather, he must cultivate in people's souls the fear of God, and plant in their hearts awe of Him, glorified be He, in the unseen. This is the true watcher, the constant watcher who never leaves you and never parts from you for an instant.

Therefore, the woman whom a man sought to seduce, enticing her with the claim that they were in a desert where no one could see them, and he said to her: "What prevents you from me, and what sees us but the stars?" She said to him: "You fool, where is the Star of stars?" This is the fear of the Merciful in the unseen.

It is narrated that al-Mu'tadid, one of the kings of the Buyid state during the Abbasid caliphate, who was famous for intelligence and justice, once had a man come to the market of Baghdad to sell a precious necklace so he could perform the Hajj with its price. He found no buyer in the market because of the necklace's preciousness. The man passed by a dignified elder who bore signs of righteousness, and he said: "This is a trustworthy man; I will entrust this necklace to him as a deposit until I return from the Hajj." When he returned from the Hajj, he asked the elder about the necklace he had left with him, but the elder denied it, and all his attempts to recover the necklace failed.

One of the passersby heard him and said: "Sir, he is a deceitful liar. Go to al-Mu'tadid, and he will return the necklace to you by his intelligence and cunning." The man went to al-Mu'tadid and related the story to him. He said: "Go tomorrow and sit beside this man, and I will pass by you in my procession. Do not stand for me, and if I speak to you, respond while seated, and leave this matter to me."

The next day al-Mu'tadid passed by in his awe-inspiring procession, with his retinue, his pomp, and his staff. He looked at the owner of the necklace and said: "O so-and-so, since when have you been here? How is it that you did not inform me of your presence so that I could meet you and give you your due?"

When the elder heard these words, he thought the man was one of the king's acquaintances and followers, so he trembled, called out to the owner of the necklace, and said: "I beg you, do not mention me before the king with this story of the necklace." He went to the necklace and returned it to its owner. The man took the necklace to al-Mu'tadid, who smiled and said to him: "Wait for me tomorrow in front of this man's shop."

Indeed, al-Mu'tadid came the next day, but this time he had with him the gallows. He ordered it erected in front of this deceiver's shop, and ordered him hanged. Then he said: "This is the reward of one whose faith is witnessed among people, and not his faith in the unseen," meaning: far from the eyes of people.

Therefore God placed the hypocrites in the lowest level of the Fire, though they were the first of people to hasten to prayer and were in the first row behind the Messenger of God. Yet this was their recompense. Why? Because the hypocrite is inconsistent with himself: his tongue contradicts his heart.

Among the meanings of "the unseen" in His saying, ﴿وَخشِيَ ٱلرَّحْمـٰنَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ﴾ [Yasin: 11], is: the unseen that God has informed us of, namely that there is an Afterlife, resurrection, gathering, and reckoning.

This khashyah toward God is with the unseen, meaning: faith in the unseen. We believe in God, glorified be He, while He is unseen. The unseen, as we have said, is what is hidden from you, and there is no path in the universe that leads you to it, nor any preliminaries. For example, in solving geometry exercises or theory we know: the hypothesis, the givens, and the required. The givens and premises lead you to the goal and the required.

Therefore you find that knowledge of the unseen divides into two parts: an unseen that God has reserved for Himself, which He does not reveal to anyone except whom He approves of among the Messengers, and for which He has not made any preliminaries leading to it or indicating it; and an unseen that has preliminaries which point you to it. If you use these preliminaries, you reach through them today what was unseen yesterday. You should infer, from the unseen that has become visible to you, that you should believe in the unseen whose reality you have not grasped and for which you have no way, and what you see should move you to believe in what you have not seen.

We have said that this second kind of unseen, the unseen that has preliminaries leading to it, has a birth in which it appears. If that birth coincides with a human search, and the search is the cause of its appearance, well and good; otherwise God manifests it by coincidence, as most discoveries that serve humanity today have come by coincidence, because the birth of the unseen came while your search for it had not come.

The believer is one whose faith in the unseen increases when he infers from what has appeared to him what has not appeared. Among scholars and gifted people are those who explain to you an unseen that has not yet come due by something already existing in fact. Among this is what is narrated: the Romans sent to the Commander of the Faithful asking him to send them a scholar who would instruct them in matters of religion. He sent them al-Sha'bi, and they began asking him about what was hidden from them in religion. Among what they put to him was that a person, when blessed in Paradise, eats and does not defecate; how can that be? Al-Sha'bi answered with the illuminating insights that God opens to whomever He wills. He said to them: "Have you seen the fetus in its mother's womb? It is nourished and grows without defecating, and if it defecated in its placenta it would burn. Likewise the person in Paradise eats and does not defecate, because he is nourished by God's provision for him. God gives him in measure such that nothing remains that a person would excrete. As for us, we eat by our own provisioning for ourselves, and we do not eat in measure of need, so we defecate."

They said to him: "You claim that you take from Paradise whatever you wish without anything being diminished from it. How is that?" He said: "A thing diminishes by being taken from when it has no replenishment from elsewhere; if it has a replenishment, it does not diminish, and the replenishment in Paradise is from God, so how could diminishing occur?"

Another thing: if you come to a lamp and take from it a flame, nay, thousands of flames, does any light diminish from the lamp?

Thus al-Sha'bi replied, and the people admired him. They wrote him a letter to bring to the Commander of the Faithful, and it seems they envied the Commander of the Faithful that such an intellect and talent should be in his service. The letter said: "I wonder at a people among whom is someone like al-Sha'bi, how would they appoint anyone else?"

When al-Sha'bi went and handed the letter to him, the Commander of the Faithful read it and said to al-Sha'bi: "Do you know what is in the letter?" He said: "No, Commander of the Faithful." He said: "Read." Al-Sha'bi read the sentence: "I wonder at a people among whom is someone like al-Sha'bi, how would they appoint anyone else?" He said: "Yes, Commander of the Faithful, because they have not seen you, and if they had seen you, they would have changed their opinion."

One who reflects on the matter of warning finds that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had two kinds of warning: a general warning to all the worlds, which is a warning of delivery from God to everyone, believer and disbeliever, and about which God said: ﴿إِنَّآ أَرْسَلْنَاكَ بِٱلْحَقِّ بَشِيراً وَنَذِيراً..﴾ [Fatir: 24]. Those who believe in God benefit from the warning and benefit from the good news, while those who do not believe gain nothing from that.

The other warning is a specific warning for those who fear the Merciful in the unseen, the warning of acceptance, from which benefits whoever fears the Merciful in the unseen. Those who do not fear their Lord were warned earlier, but by a warning of delivery, so they did not benefit from it; therefore the specific warning did not include them.

As for His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿فَبَشِّرْهُ بِمَغْفِرَةٍ وَأَجْرٍ كَرِيمٍ﴾ [Yasin: 11], we have said that good news is informing of good before its time, to motivate you toward the causes of good and to make you eager for them. You notice here that forgiveness precedes the reward. Why? They said: because the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, before giving you the blessing, first removes punishment from you, since clearing away precedes adorning, as we have said. Moreover, forgiveness is always the recompense for faith in God, while the reward is the recompense for acting by God's method. Therefore He, glorified be He, said: ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لاَ يَغْفِرُ أَن يُشْرَكَ بِهِ وَيَغْفِرُ مَا دُونَ ذَلِكَ لِمَن يَشَآءُ﴾ [An-Nisa: 48]. Whoever believes in God is secure from punishment and guaranteed forgiveness; if he wants the reward, he must do righteous deeds.

The reward itself is described as "generous" (karim), though the Generous is the Giver, glorified be He. The meaning is that the generosity of the Giver extended to the gift, so the gift became generous, as if it yearns for its owner, just as a man yearns for giving. Therefore we have said: the blessing that God bestows upon His creation loves its owner, seeks him out, and dislikes whoever envies him for it or bears spite toward him because of it.

Therefore, do not go to this envious, spiteful person, and no good from it will ever reach him, as if the Bestower, glorified be He, is saying: as long as you have disliked the blessing in the possession of another, you will attain nothing from it, because you are finding fault with God in His giving and objecting to His decree, so how would His blessing come to you? But if you love the blessing in the possession of another, it will come to you and knock on your door itself.

This matter has many examples from our lives. I mention that a man from our town of Mit Ghamr came to me complaining of the harshness of his wealthy uncle toward him, and that despite his riches, he was stingy with him. He was employing strangers and leaving him without work, and other things he mentioned in his complaint. My family was present at this sitting, and one of them said to him: "My son, you always curse your uncle and speak ill of his rights." He said: "Yes, because he does not ask about me."

I said to him: "I will ask you a question and make you swear not to lie." When he saw that I would have him swear on the Qur'an, he backed down. I said: "Do you love the blessing in your uncle's possession?" He said: "No, how could I love it, when I receive none of it?" I said: "If you loved the blessing in your uncle's possession, and wished him goodness and increase, the blessing would come knocking at your door." He said: "Then please, sir, speak to my uncle and recommend me to him."

It seems the man truly tried to reform himself, and God set right what was between him and his uncle. After the dawn prayer he came knocking at the door, and when he entered he said, weeping: "Sir, let me tell you a story stranger than fiction." I said: "What is it?" He said: "An hour before dawn, someone knocked hard on my door. I got up and opened it, and there was my uncle rebuking me, saying: 'How do you leave me to strangers who plunder my wealth while you are busy with your own affairs? Take the keys, and from the morning open the shops and attend to my interests yourself.'"

I said to him: "Yes, because you loved the blessing in your uncle's possession and changed what you harbored in your soul toward him. So: whoever wishes that all the blessings of people be with him, let him love the blessing in another's possession."

Then the Exalted says:

﴿إِنَّا نَحْنُ نُحْيِي ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ وَنَكْتُبُ مَا قَدَّمُواْ وَآثَارَهُمْ...﴾ [Yasin: 12]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 36, verse 12:

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾. "Innā" and "naḥnu" are two pronouns of the speaker, used in the manner of glorification (ta'ẓīm). "Innā" is in fact "naḥnu," just as if you said: Zayd is Zayd. So what did "naḥnu" add after "innā"? The rule in the construction of the language is that distinguishing a thing (tamyīz) occurs when there is partnership (ishtirāk); if there is no partnership, distinguishing does not occur... It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, when He said "innā," and there was no one else, said "innā naḥnu," meaning: as if He said "innā, innā," meaning: no one but Me. So there is no partnership in this matter.

We have already explained that the speech of Allah about Himself may come in the plural form, as in:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

And He said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We are its guardians﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9]. You notice that the pronoun here is for glorification. Likewise in every verse that speaks of one of His acts, or of one of His bounties, because every act of His, glorified is He, requires several attributes: it requires knowledge, wisdom, power, and so on. All these attributes are contained in "naḥnu," which indicates the complete majesty found in Allah's Most Beautiful Names.

As for when He, glorified is He, speaks of the single Essence, He uses the first-person singular pronoun, as in:

﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 14]. He did not say, for example: "Indeed, we are Allah," because "innā" and "naḥnu" indicate plurality, and the speech here concerns oneness, so it must come in the singular form.

For this reason, the Truth, glorified is He, affirms this oneness by several means of emphasis in His words, glorified is He:

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but I, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 14]. He did not say, glorified is He: "So worship Us and establish prayer for Our remembrance," but rather "So worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance" [Ṭā-Hā: 14], because worship is due to Allah alone.

Furthermore, the process of resurrection and the bringing of the dead to life belongs to Allah alone; none shares it with Him.

He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ — with "the recording" mentioned after "the bringing to life," even though recording precedes the process of bringing to life. The recording was in this world, and the bringing to life is in the Hereafter, so why? Firstly: you must note that this speech is not your speech but the speech of Allah, so you must use your intellect to understand from Allah His intended meaning, because the style of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, carries the perfections that suit His perfection, while your speech carries what suits your perfection.

For this reason we have said previously that the Qur'an has distinctions over all books, and that its treatment is different from the treatment of any book...

So what is the wisdom in placing ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾ before ﴿and We record what they have sent forward﴾? They said: because what is the benefit of recording? Recording of deeds is to count the good deeds so that we reward for them, and to count the bad deeds so that we punish for them. If there is no bringing of the dead to life, reckoning and recompense, then what is the benefit of recording? Therefore the bringing to life was placed before the recording of deeds, just as the bringing to life is greater than the recording, so it was fitting that it precede it.

The meaning of "what they have sent forward" (mā qaddamū) is: the deeds. A deed may be a fruitful, continuing work after the death of its doer, such as ongoing charity (ṣadaqah jāriyah). If a person, for example, digs a well from which people drink, and he dies, the well continues to give people water; or if he leaves beneficial knowledge. All of this is one of the traces (āthār) of the deed that was recorded first, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿and their traces﴾.

Among a person's traces is what he established for people and left to be followed after him, whether it is good or evil. All of it is written and recorded in a Book that leaves nothing small or great unaccounted for, and it has counted their traces after their owner. If a person, for example, writes an unjust will that deprives the rightful owner of his right, or deprives the heir of his inheritance, its effects bear all the consequences of this injustice; for he has not only deprived the direct heir, but also deprived his descendants who would have benefited from this inheritance. Therefore its burden remains upon him until the Day of Resurrection.

Likewise, whoever establishes for people an unjust law bears the burden of the unjust law that he ruled by, and then the burden of whoever rules by this law after him. Take, for example, the matter of the public sector: whoever established it established it, and then its effects continued to plunder people until everyone cried out against it, and the rulers themselves demanded its amendment.

This matter explains to us the saying of our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection, and whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection."

Have you seen the old man who plants a palm tree, and perhaps does not benefit from its fruit, but whoever comes after him benefits from it? These are his traces after him; Allah records them for him and counts them for his reckoning.

Some scholars said, regarding the meaning of ﴿and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾: that is, We record what they sent forward of intention (niyyah), which precedes the deed, and then We record the deed itself, which is the traces of this intention. So when you form an intention of good in a deed, you take the reward of the intention, and when you do the deed, you take the reward of the deed.

This explains to us the noble hadith: "Whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him; and whoever intends it and does it, ten [good deeds] are recorded for him." This guides us to the importance of forming the intention before beginning the deed, so that a person may be rewarded for it; the believer does not undertake deeds haphazardly.

As for His words: ﴿And We have counted everything in a clear Register (imām mubīn)﴾: there is a difference between recording (kitābah) and counting (iḥṣā'). Recording is that you write a thing, but you do not gather the written items together, so there is a need for one who counts and numbers them. Thus the Truth, glorified is He, records our deeds first in writing, then in counting and enumeration; and counting and enumeration are also in a recorded Book in which everything is contained, ﴿in a clear Register (imām mubīn)﴾. The imām is that which is followed, and what is meant here is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), from which the angels take their task in managing the universe.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 36, verse 15:

When they denied and rejected (the messengers) a second time, it was necessary to emphasize the speech in this manner: ﴿Indeed, we are sent to you as messengers.﴾ Every word in this phrase carries emphasis: first with (inna) "indeed," then the style of restriction (qasr) in fronting the prepositional phrase ilaykum, "to you," then the emphatic lam (lam al-tawkid) in (lamursalun), "are sent." So, emphasis is proportional to denial. And these people deny the message on several grounds. First: ﴿They said, "You are nothing but humans like us."﴾ [Yasin: 15]. Then: ﴿The Most Merciful has not sent down anything.﴾ [Yasin: 15]. Then: ﴿You are only lying.﴾ [Yasin: 15].

Their saying ﴿You are nothing but humans like us﴾ [Yasin: 15] reflects their view that the humanity of the messengers is a flaw in the message. But how can the message be realized if the messenger is not a human?

God, glorified is He, discusses this matter elsewhere, saying:

﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, except that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?" Say: "If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ [al-Isra: 94-95].

This is the first response to them: those who walk on the earth are humans, not angels.

And at another place God accommodates Himself to the creatures, saying: ﴿Even if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. That is, even if the messenger came as an angel, he would necessarily descend in the form of a human, "and otherwise how would you see him? And how would you receive from him in his angelic form?"

Therefore, it is necessary that the messenger be of the same kind as those to whom he is sent, so that exemplary conduct (uswa) in him is valid. How can exemplary conduct be realized in an angel messenger, who does not disobey God at all, whereas the messenger is required to convey the methodology of God and to implement it himself? Therefore God, glorified is He, said: ﴿Certainly you have in the Messenger of God an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], meaning: he himself implements the method he brought before he conveys it to the people.

Their saying ﴿The Most Merciful has not sent down anything﴾ [Yasin: 15] shows their foolishness in reasoning. It is strange of them to acknowledge God, exalted is He, with the attribute of mercy while they do not believe in Him. Among the requirements of this mercy is that He send to them a messenger who guides them to good and protects them from evil. So, they acknowledge the premise that condemns them, then go further and accuse the messengers of lying: ﴿You are only lying﴾ [Yasin: 15].

At this point the messengers affirm their message, saying: ﴿Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you.﴾ The phrase "our Lord knows" (rabbuna ya'lamu) takes the place of an oath, because they call God to witness the truth of their message, and oaths among the Arabs serve to establish a disputed matter. Since the messengers said "our Lord knows," the matter is either true or not true; if it is not true, then they have lied about God...

These disbelievers, in their denial of the messengers, believe that by doing so they are zealous for God and avenge themselves on the messengers who lie about Him, glorified is He. So they say:

﴿They said, "We see an evil omen in you. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you...﴾
