كأنهم يقولون للرسل: ما دُمْتم كذبتم على الله وقلتم ﴿رَبُّنَا يَعْلَمُ..﴾ [يس: ١٦] في أمور نظنكم فيها كاذبين، فقد تطيَّرنا بكم، يعني: تشاءمنا. والتطيُّر من الطَّيَرة (التشاؤم بالطير أو بغيره من الفأل السيئ). وكانت عادة معروفة عند العرب، فكانوا حين يريد الواحد منهم عمل شيء، يأتي إلى طير فيزجره ويُطلقه، فيرى إلى أين يطير: فإنْ طار إلى اليمين أمضى ما ينوي عليه، وإنْ طار إلى اليسار أمسك وتشاءم، وقد حرَّم الإسلامُ هذه العادة ونهى عنها.

وقولهم ﴿لَئِن لَّمْ تَنتَهُواْ﴾ [يس: ١٨]، أي: عما تقولونه من أنكم مُرسَلون بمنهج، ﴿لَنَرْجُمَنَّكُمْ وَلَيَمَسَّنَّكُمْ مِّنَّا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ [يس: ١٨]، فجمعوا عليهم الرجم والعذاب الأليم، والرجم غير العذاب، فالرجم رَمْيٌ بالحجارة حتى الموت، فهو إنهاءٌ للعذاب؛ لأن التعذيب إيلامُ حيٍّ، فمَن مات لا تستطيع أن تُعذِّبه، لذلك قالت العرب: لا يضير الشاةَ سلخُها بعد ذبحها.

لذلك لما ادَّعى أحد القضاة أن القرآن ليس فيه نصٌّ على الرجم: قلنا لهم: صحيح، ليس في القرآن آيةٌ تنص على الرجم، لكن أيهما أقوى في التقنين (التشريع): الكلام أم الفعل؟ أيهما يُعَدُّ حُجة؟ لا شكَّ أن الفعل أقوى حجة، لأن الكلام يمكن أن يُؤوَّل، أمَّا الفعل فلا تأويل فيه، وقد فعل الرسول ﷺ الرجم في ماعز والغامدية.

إذن: الاحتجاج هنا ليس بالنصِّ القولي، وإنما بالفعل من رسول الله الذي فوَّضه الله في أن يشرِّع، وأمرنا بطاعة أوامره، فقال سبحانه: ﴿وَمَآ آتَاكُمُ ٱلرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَٱنتَهُواْ﴾ [الحشر: ٧]، والحق سبحانه لا يأمرنا هذا الأمر إلا إذا كان قد ترك لرسول الله أموراً يُشرِّعها.

وهذه من مزاياه ﷺ على غيره من الرسل، فكل رسول ما عليه إلا أن يُبلِّغ الحكم كما جاءه من الله، أمَّا سيدنا رسول الله فأُمر أن يُبلِّغ عن الله، وترك له بعض الأمور، وفوَّض أن يشرِّع فيها.

لذلك جاءت هذه الآية: ﴿وَمَآ آتَاكُمُ ٱلرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَٱنتَهُواْ﴾ [الحشر: ٧].

لذلك حين نستقرئ آيات الطاعة تجد القرآن يقول مرة: ﴿وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱلرَّسُولَ﴾ [المائدة: ٩٢].

ويقول في آية أخرى: ﴿وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَٱلرَّسُولَ﴾ [آل عمران: ١٣٢].

ويقول: ﴿وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱلرَّسُولَ﴾ [النساء: ٥٩].

فتكرار الفعل (أَطِيعُوا) يعني: أن الجهة منفكَّة، فلله تعالى أمر، وللرسول أمر، يعني: أطيعوا الله في التقنين الإجمالي العام، وأطيعوا الرسول في تفصيل ما أُجمل، ففي الزكاة مثلاً جاء الأمر العام بأداء الزكاة، لكن لم يحدد الحق سبحانه لها نصاباً، وهذا النِّصاب بيَّنه سيدنا رسول الله. إذن: لله فيها أمر، وللرسول أمر.

أما إن جاء الأمر (وأطيعوا) واحداً وعُطف رسول الله على الله، ولم تُكرر الطاعة مع المطاع، فاعلم أن الأمر واحد قاله الله وقاله رسول الله، فطاعة المطاع الثاني من باطن طاعة المطاع الأول، كما في قوله سبحانه: ﴿أَطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱلرَّسُولَ وَأُوْلِي ٱلأَمْرِ مِنْكُمْ﴾ [النساء: ٥٩]، فلم يقل: وأطيعوا أولي الأمر منكم؛ لأن طاعة أولي الأمر من باطن طاعة الله وطاعة رسوله، وليس لهم طاعة مستقلة منفصلة، بل طاعتهم في ظلِّ طاعة الله وطاعة رسوله.

إذن: الاستدلال بالفعل أقوى من الاستدلال بالقول، فإن قال قائل: نريد أن نسمع كلام الله في هذه المسألة، نقول: نعم، هناك كلام بالنصِّ وكلام باللازم (أي ما يُستلزم ضمناً)، والحق سبحانه حين تكلم عن الإماء في هذه المسألة قال: ﴿فَعَلَيْهِنَّ نِصْفُ مَا عَلَى ٱلْمُحْصَنَٰتِ مِنَ ٱلْعَذَابِ﴾ [النساء: ٢٥].

والعذاب كما قلنا: إيلامُ حيٍّ، أمَّا الرجم فهو إنهاءٌ للحياة، وإنهاءٌ للعذاب؛ لذلك بيَّن الحق سبحانه أن النصف للعذاب، وهنا يُخرِج الرجم؛ لأن الرجم لا يُنصَّف. إذن: فالنصف ليس على الإطلاق، وكونه يخصُّ هنا العذاب، فهذا يعني أن عليهن الرجم أيضاً كاملاً، لا يُنصَّف.

ومن ذلك أيضاً قوله تعالى في قصة سليمان عليه السلام والهدهد: ﴿لأُعَذِّبَنَّهُ عَذَاباً شَدِيداً أَوْ لأَاْذبَحَنَّهُ﴾ [النمل: ٢١]، إذن: العذاب غير الذبح وغير القتل.

وقولهم: ﴿لَنَرْجُمَنَّكُمْ﴾ [يس: ١٨]، الرجم قد يُطلق على القول، لنرجمنَّكم بالقول، وقد يكون الرجم على حقيقته بشدة حتى الموت، أو بهوادة، فيُراد منه الإيلام.

"Their omen is with themselves." That is: their ill omen (tashā'um) is with them, i.e., inseparable from them. What is meant here is disbelief. The first hamza in ﴿أَئِن﴾ is the interrogative particle, and ﴿إِن﴾ is a conditional particle whose response is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Is it that when you are reminded of God and of the path of your Creator, and of what makes you happy in your worldly life, the result is that you threaten the one who reminds you with stoning and painful punishment, instead of blessing him, supporting him, and following what he has brought you?"

﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed all bounds.﴾ That is: transgressing the limit. For the matter between us and you has not gone beyond being a verbal debate, in which we have not overstepped the bounds of conveying the message, namely that we are sent to you. The result was that you met this verbal debate with this harsh, extravagant act that exceeds all limits, as you have gathered against us stoning and painful punishment.

At this point, what happened?

﴿And there came a man running from the farthest part of the city.﴾ He said....

The Qur'anic verse and the commentary on it: "And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running. He said, 'O my people, follow the messengers.'"

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah Yasin, verse 20:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ indicates that the first two messengers, whom the people denied, had believing supporters who affirmed their call. When the third came and the people also denied him, the zeal for truth (ḥamiyyat al-ḥaqq) seized those believers, and among them was this man who came from the farthest part of the city, running to support the truth and raise its word.

In this verse we notice, first, His saying: ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾, that he was not near the place of this verbal debate, and that he bore hardships in the cause of supporting the truth. This is evidence of the strength of faith (al-ṭāqa al-īmāniyya) in this man, and also evidence that the call of the two earlier messengers had reached the farthest part of the city.

Then He described him as "a man" (rajul) and did not say "so-and-so," thereby mentioning the prominent attribute in his make-up, that he is a man.

The aspiration (himma) of a man is what determines the measure of his manhood. A man who wants life for himself alone, and everyone serves him, who sees everything for himself and does not see himself for anyone, this is a man whose homeland is himself and his essence. And a man whose homeland is his family and dependents, to whom he extends his benefit. And a man whose homeland is his nation. And a man whose homeland is the whole world, like our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the philosophy of manhood.

Therefore: the aspirations of men determine their homelands and their ranks, and the highest of these ranks is the man whose homeland is the whole world, because all creation are the dependents of Allah. Whoever loves good for them and scatters upon them what benefits them has been entrusted by Allah with the provision of the servants.

To illustrate this, we say: suppose you have children. One of them takes his allowance and spends it on his pleasures, desires and what is of no benefit; and another uses his allowance to buy sweets and distributes them among his young siblings. Which of them would you then prefer, and which would you increase? Likewise, the hand that distributes on behalf of Allah to the creation of Allah, as if Allah were saying to him: "You are trusted with My blessing, trusted with My creation." And from this is the saying of the poet:

His saying "running" (yas'ā) means that his coming was not ordinary; rather he came hastening, racing. "He said, 'O my people, follow the messengers.'" His saying "O my people" is a call intended to evoke tenderness in the one addressed, as if he were saying: "O my family, O my kin, O my sons," thereby mentioning the bonds of affection and mercy between him and them.

His saying "follow the messengers" indicates his support for them, and here he mentions the first ground for this following: that they are messengers.

Then he mentions to them another justification, saying: "Follow those who ask you no reward, and they are rightly guided" (Yasin 36:21). That is, they did not seek any wage from you for their call.

The phrase "those who ask you no reward" is only used when the work carried out requires a reward, and the Messenger came only to benefit those to whom he was sent. Logically, then, his work calls for a reward. But who can repay him? No one can repay him except God, because the Messenger's benefit extends beyond the benefit of this world to the benefit of the Hereafter. Which of mankind can give the Messenger what he deserves?

For this reason we see all the Messengers saying this same statement: "My reward is only with God" (Yunus 10:72). That is, "You people do not possess the measure of my reward, nor can you assess it; rather, the one for whose sake I work gives me my reward." All of God's Messengers said this statement except two: Our master Abraham and our master Moses, peace be upon them both. Why?

They said: Because Abraham's first call was to his father Azar, and it was not fitting that he should ask him for a reward for calling him to the truth. Likewise, our master Moses, when he first called, called Pharaoh, who had raised him in his house and to whom he owed a favour, so how could he ask him for a reward?

As for His saying, glorified is He: "and they are rightly guided" (Yasin 36:21), this is a third justification for following them: they are sent by the One who sent them, and God sends only one who guides to the straight path that leads to Him, glorified is He. These Messengers are rightly guided in themselves, and consequently they guide others. So He is mentioning the matter and its cause: these Messengers ask no reward and do not call to error, but to guidance.

Then this man turns to himself and says to his people: "I am not commanding you to something from which I myself am removed. And if I were to advise you sincerely, I would not betray myself. And why should I not worship He who originated me?" (Yasin 36:22). That is, He created me from nothing, so He is more deserving of worship. He is the One who made me, brought me into existence from non-existence, and has continually bestowed His blessings upon me. So what prevents me from worshipping Him, when He is more deserving of worship? And even if my worship of Him were only to repay Him for His blessings, without regard to reward, His worship would still be obligatory.

This is not the speech of a Messenger; it is the speech of a believing man who volunteered, in whose heart faith had taken hold, and who wished to purify his faith and to extend his guidance to others, in keeping with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself."

God, glorified is He, created the creation first, then sent the Messengers with the method for their guidance. The Messengers in turn conveyed it to their companions, and whoever received something from it bore it just as the Messenger bore it. Therefore the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God make radiant the face of a man who hears my saying, memorises it, and then conveys it to one who has not heard it, for many a bearer of knowledge is more retentive than a hearer."

So the responsibility for the call is borne first by the Messengers, and then by the believers in them to whom the call has reached. This bearing is not a favour; it is a charge from God. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: "That you may be witnesses over mankind, and that the Messenger may be a witness over you" (al-Baqarah 2:143). Just as the Messenger bore witness that he had conveyed to you, it is incumbent upon you to bear witness to people that you have conveyed to them, because the believers in the message are an extension of the Messenger.

Therefore, we see this believing man who came from the farthest part of the city, striving to raise the word of truth and to support the Messengers, was not a Messenger, and no one had charged him with this; rather, he volunteered for it, because the power of faith within him drove him to this stance.

Then he applies the matter to himself first, saying: "And why should I not worship He who created me, and to Him you will be returned?" This is a gentle way of presenting the call, and more likely to be accepted.

His saying "And why should I not" is as if he is marvelling at his own situation, were he not to believe in the One who originated him. Wondering at oneself is among the most truthful forms of expression: it is as though he is neither disputing nor flattering, but saying what is in his own soul, just as our master Sulayman (peace be upon him) said: "Why do I not see the hoopoe?" [al-Naml: 20].

So the answer does not lie with others but with himself. It is as if he says: the hoopoe must be present, but I do not see it. The rule is that he uses the general term, and the whole is present, so the wonder is in me: "Why do I not see it?" Then he repeats the matter: "Or is it among the absent?" [al-Naml: 20], meaning: either the obstacle is from me, or from it. He casts doubt on the first, then examines carefully and finds it is from himself.

So his saying "And why should I not worship He who created me, and to Him you will be returned" is as if the matter of origination and creation requires that you worship the One who originated you, and departing from this is a matter that calls for wonder.

For this reason, in Surat al-Baqarah, the Exalted addresses us in addressing the disbelievers:

"How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life?" [al-Baqarah: 28], meaning: how could that come from you? Your disbelief in Allah, who created you and provided for you, is something that is not permissible by rational logic, so tell us, then, the way in which you disbelieved.

Al-Fatr (origination): the wondrous creation without a previous pattern. Therefore He, glorified, says of Himself: "The Originator of the heavens and the earth" [al-Baqarah: 117], meaning: He created the heavens and the earth at the outset, without a prior pattern that He followed in creation.

Or: the meaning of "He who originated me" is that [I worship Him] in faith to Him, a faith of natural disposition (fitrah). So his belief in Allah is either a belief of gratitude to the One who created him and brought him into being without a prior pattern, or the belief of the original natural disposition upon which Allah created people, and which he responded to because of this disposition within his own self.

When we reflect on the mission of this man, we find that he is like the heart in relation to the rest of the body's members, that is, in terms of the formation of the stages of faith. How? The body is made up of many limbs, each limb has its importance and function, and the life of the body requires the means of life: food, drink and air. A person eats from the produce of the earth and drinks from its water...

Likewise, this man, in terms of the strength of his faith: after he believed and faith settled in his heart, he wished to extend his faith to his people, and to shine upon them with the guidance with which his heart had been saturated... His saying, the Exalted, "and to Him you will be returned," means: do not think that you will escape from Allah, for you are in His grip; you were at the beginning from Him by your own admission, and likewise the end will be to Him and the return. If you do not appreciate the blessing of bringing into being, then appreciate the consequence of returning.

We note in this verse that the believing man speaks of himself in the singular, "And why should I not worship He who created me," then he shifts from the singular to address the group and the denying people, "and to Him you will be returned," and he did not say, "and to Him I will return." Why?

They said: because obedience, which is the root of worship, comes in three stages:

The first: that you obey one in whom you find a perfect model that deserves to be obeyed and praised for his perfection, even if nothing from him returns to you. As, for example, you look at a wonderful, expressive poem and admire its composer and commend him; nothing from it returns to you, but you esteem the poet for his own sake.

The second: that you obey a person and esteem him for a benefit that returns to you from him. We often see people serving a coward who does not deserve to be served, and people only serve him out of greed for what he has.

The third stage: that you obey a person or respect him merely out of fear of him and to guard against his evil.

The man who came from the farthest part of the city, striving, achieved the first and second stages in his saying, "And why should I not worship He who created me": I worship Him because in His perfection He deserves to be worshipped, and I worship Him for His continuous blessings. As for the third stage, he assigned it to these disbelieving people of his, so he said, "and to Him you will be returned."

That is: be alert, O people. If you do not esteem in Allah the attributes of perfection for which He is loved, and do not esteem in Allah His continuous blessings upon you, then know that the return to Him, the coming back and the destination are in His hands, and He, glorified, is powerful over you, and none escapes from His grip.

Then this believing man emphasises the matter of worshipping Allah alone, adding:

"Shall I take besides Him gods, if the Most Merciful should intend for me some harm, their intercession will avail me nothing at all..."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 36, verse 23:

The interrogative in ﴿أَأَتَّخِذُ﴾ ("Shall I take...?") carries the meaning of wonder and denial. He is amazed and rejects the idea of how one could take gods besides Allah, when it is Allah who created him. When you reflect on the meaning of the verb (ittakhadha, "to take"), you find that the thing taken is not essentially so. The meaning of taking gods is that they are not gods in reality, and that they do not deserve to be gods, but you have deliberately turned them into gods... Therefore, since these are gods that have been taken, the meaning is that they have no existence at all, as if the man is correcting his people's notion of worship.

As for His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿إِن يُرِدْنِ الرَّحْمَـٰنُ بِضُرٍّ﴾ ("If the Most Merciful wills me harm..."), this expression contains a subtle point that should be pondered, because the attribute of mercy in al-Rahman seems to contradict harm, so how did the context bring the two together?

We say: if you interpret what Allah's decree brings upon you as harm to you, understand that it comes from the Most Merciful. There must be wisdom in the One who brings it upon you, who is al-Rahman, in what He has ordained. Therefore we say: "My Lord, I praise You for all Your judgment and all Your decree, a praise of contentment with Your rule, out of certainty in Your wisdom."

So it is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to you: be aware that not everything you see as harmful by your own laws is so; for the One who brings it upon you is al-Rahman, and within this harm lies much benefit. Just as a tender father brings his child to the doctor, who performs a painful operation, or removes a part of him to heal the rest of the body, this is harm in appearance, but in reality it is mercy towards him...

Thus, the lesson we wish to dwell upon in this verse is that if al-Rahman seems to you to contradict the act of harm, this is so in your own view; in the view of the One who brings it about, there is no contradiction, because it stems from His mercy (al-Rahmaniyyah).

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿لَّا تُغْنِ عَنِّي شَفَاعَتُهُمْ شَيْئًا﴾ ("Their intercession will avail me nothing at all"), it means: the intercession of these gods, if they had any intercession, will be of no use, because they are partners of Allah and rivals to Allah, so how could their intercession be accepted by Him, glory be to Him?

A condition for intercession is that the intercessor be beloved to the one interceded with. These gods, even supposing they had any intercession, would not be accepted by Allah, the Exalted. Yet these gods in themselves are excused, since they have no sin; they did not claim to be gods, rather it was humans who claimed that.

We have already mentioned that these gods disowned being worshipped besides Allah, and the poet who expressed this meaning spoke well, saying on behalf of these gods:

As for His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿وَلَا يُنقِذُونَ﴾ ("nor can they save me"), this is because an intercessor whose intercession is rejected may be able to save the one interceded for from the hand of the one interceded with; but as for these gods, their intercession is not accepted, and they cannot save anyone who asks them to intercede for him.

We have explained the meaning of intercession (shafa'ah), and that it derives from shaf' (pair, "even"): a person has a matter and cannot resolve it alone by the means at his disposal, so he seeks help from another to support him and join him to strengthen him in resolving it. Thus, having been single, he becomes a pair with the intercessor, that is, two...

Therefore, these gods, even supposing they had intercession, it is rejected and unaccepted intercession; and they also cannot save whoever seeks refuge in them from the grip of the Truth, glory be to Him. They are fit neither for intercession nor for rescue...

The question in ﴿أَأَتَّخِذُ﴾ [Yasin: 23] carries the meaning of wonder and denial. He is amazed and rejects the idea: how could one take gods besides God, when it is God who created him? When you reflect on the meaning of the verb (atakhadha, "to take"), you find that the thing taken is not essentially so. The meaning of taking gods is that they are not gods in reality, and that they do not deserve to be gods; yet you have resorted to them and made them gods. Similar to this is the taking of a son in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He did not take any son, nor was there any god with Him; otherwise each god would have run off with what he created..﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

The meaning is that God, may He be exalted, has no son in reality. If you say that God has taken a son, this means that He came upon a child and adopted him, exalted is God far above that by a great exaltation. Just as you say, "I took a son," meaning: you came upon a child you did not bear and adopted him.

Therefore: since these are gods that have been taken, the meaning is that they have no existence at all, and it is as if the man is correcting his people's notion of worship.

As for His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me﴾ [Yasin: 23], this phrase contains a subtle point that deserves reflection, because the attribute of mercy in "the Most Merciful" seems to contradict harm, so how did the context bring the two together?

We say: if you interpret what the decree of God brings upon you as harm to you, then understand that it comes from the Most Merciful, so there must be wisdom in what He who brings it upon you, the Most Merciful, has caused to happen. Therefore we say: "I praise You, my Lord, for all Your judgment and all Your decree, a praise of contentment with Your rule, out of certainty in Your wisdom."

It is as if the Truth, may He be glorified, is saying to you: be mindful that not everything that you see as harmful according to your own laws is so; for the one who brings it upon you is the Most Merciful, and within the folds of this harm there is much benefit. Just as a tender father takes his son to the doctor, who performs a painful operation on him or removes a part of him to repair the rest of the body; this is harm in appearance, and in reality it is mercy towards him.

Therefore we have said before: if your son comes in bleeding, do not receive this except with contentment, not with anger, until you have asked about the one who did it. If he was an enemy, you may be angry with him; if he was a loving one, you accept what happened with contentment, and you say to the child: surely your uncle, for example, saw you making a mistake and punished you.

Likewise, do not judge God's decrees that He brings upon you except from the standpoint that they come from the Most Merciful, who is more merciful to you than a mother to her child, and you are His creation and His handiwork. We have never seen any of the foolish of mankind deliberately break his own handiwork; rather he takes care of it, and applies the hand of beautification and adornment to it, just as you see the carpenter, for example, holding the plane and carving the wood. Do you say he is harming his craft? No indeed, he is improving it and beautifying it.

Therefore the Most High says in the Hadith Qudsi: "After this affection of the Creator for the creation, would He bring upon them what harms them?"

In our practical life we often see examples of this matter. You often miss the train or the bus, for example, so you take the next appointment, and on the way you find that the train or bus has had an accident, so you correct your first notion yourself, and you turn your anger at missing the train into thanks to God who saved you, when you had thought otherwise. So: look to Him who brings the decrees upon you, and do not look to superficial benefit, for God, may He be exalted, has wisdom in what He brings about, whether you know it or do not know it.

Also, one of our children often fails an exam, for example, though he has studied, striven and acquired the sciences... etc., but some obstacle, such as an illness or other, came upon him and he was not granted success. The superficial view of things says: this is evil and loss that calls for anger, God forbid, but the patient and reflective view sees God's wisdom in this failure.

So the wise father in such situations says to his son: "O my son, praise God, for you are always successful, and perhaps if you succeed this year you will not be spared the eyes of the envious; and this is an opportunity for you to increase your total so that you may enter the college you want..." etc.

Thus the father strengthens his son's bond with God, increases his faith and his contentment with his Lord, and keeps him away from anger and from discontent with the decree, and this is a matter fathers should take care to attend to.

So: the point on which we wish to pause in this verse is that if the Most Merciful seems to you to contradict the act of harm, that is in your view, but for the one who brings it about there is no contradiction, because it is of the Most Merciful.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their intercession will not avail me anything﴾ [Yasin: 23], it means: the intercession of these gods, if they had any intercession, would be of no use, because they are associates of God and rivals to God, so how would their intercession be accepted by Him, glorified be He?

It is a condition of intercession that the intercessor be beloved to the one whose intercession is sought. These gods, even on the assumption that they had some intercession, would not be accepted by God, may He be exalted. Yet these gods in themselves are excused, since they have no sin; they did not claim to be gods, rather mankind claimed that.

We have previously mentioned that these gods disowned being worshipped besides God, and the poet who put this meaning into verse spoke truly, saying in the voice of these gods:

"They worshipped us, while we are more worshipful to God than those who stand in prayer at dawn;
they wronged, in ignorance, just as they wronged the son of Mary and his disciples;
they took our silence as evidence against us, so they became fuel for the Fire;
the extremist has his recompense, and the one exaggerated about returns to salvation by the mercy of the Forgiver."

As for His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿nor will they rescue me﴾ [Yasin: 23], because when an intercessor's intercession is rejected, he may be able to rescue the one interceded for from the hand of the one interceded with; but as for these gods, their intercession is not accepted, and they cannot rescue whoever asks them to intercede for him.

We have explained the meaning of intercession, that it comes from "shaf'" (pair): a person has a matter and cannot by himself resolve it by its causes, so he seeks help from another who supports him and joins him to strengthen him in resolving it. So: after he was alone, he becomes a pair with the intercessor, that is, two.

When the Truth, may He be glorified, wished to clarify this matter for us, He said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].

And He said in another place: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123].

You notice that the beginnings of the two verses agree but their endings differ, so why? They said: because the referent of the pronoun differs. Here there is a soul that recompenses and a soul that is recompensed for; if you return the pronoun to the one recompensed for, then the one recompensed for does not intercede for himself, rather he first offers ransom and seeks to make restitution for the harm in order to pay his ransom; if ransom is not accepted from him, he then looks for one who will intercede for him. So the meaning is: no ransom is accepted from the soul itself, and the intercession of others does not benefit it.

If you return the pronoun to the recompensing soul, that is, the interceding one, then the intercessor comes forward to intercede first; if his intercession is not accepted, he offers ransom and bears the ransom.

So: these gods, on the assumption that they have intercession, their intercession is rejected and unaccepted, and they also cannot rescue those who turn to them from the grip of the Truth, may He be glorified. They are not fit for intercession or for rescue, and this meaning is clear in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it; and if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj: 73].

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in clear error﴾ [Yasin: 24], it means: if I did that and went to worshipping these gods, I would be in clear ﴿error﴾ [Yasin: 24], evident and manifest. And His saying: ﴿in clear error﴾ [Yasin: 24] is as if error surrounds him and encompasses him from every side, such that he cannot escape from it.

Then this believing man says: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾ [Yasin: 25]. This address may be directed to the messengers whom the man came to support and assist in their call; so he looked at them and said: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord﴾ [Yasin: 25], and the meaning of ﴿so listen to me﴾ [Yasin: 25] is: listen to me as to what I give you in support, and bear witness for me that I volunteered this support of faith; no one assigned me to it.

It may also be that this address is directed to the disbelieving people, so he says to them: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord﴾ [Yasin: 25], meaning: God is your Lord in spite of you; and though you disbelieve in Him, may He be glorified, I have honored His lordship over you and believed in it, to enter into the greatness of this lordship. ﴿So listen to me﴾ [Yasin: 25]: listen to me in this proclamation, so that I may have fulfilled what was obligatory upon me toward you, and delivered the message to you without deceiving or cheating you.

Then the Truth, may He be glorified, says:

﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Would that my people knew..."﴾.

The question in ﴿أَأَتَّخِذُ﴾ [Yasin: 23] carries the meaning of wonder and denial. He is amazed and rejects the idea: how could one take gods besides God, when it is God who created him? When you reflect on the meaning of the verb (atakhadha, "to take"), you find that the thing taken is not essentially so. The meaning of taking gods is that they are not gods in reality, and that they do not deserve to be gods; yet you have resorted to them and made them gods. Similar to this is the taking of a son in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He did not take any son, nor was there any god with Him; otherwise each god would have run off with what he created..﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

The meaning is that God, may He be exalted, has no son in reality. If you say that God has taken a son, this means that He came upon a child and adopted him, exalted is God far above that by a great exaltation. Just as you say, "I took a son," meaning: you came upon a child you did not bear and adopted him.

Therefore: since these are gods that have been taken, the meaning is that they have no existence at all, and it is as if the man is correcting his people's notion of worship.

As for His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me﴾ [Yasin: 23], this phrase contains a subtle point that deserves reflection, because the attribute of mercy in "the Most Merciful" seems to contradict harm, so how did the context bring the two together?

We say: if you interpret what the decree of God brings upon you as harm to you, then understand that it comes from the Most Merciful, so there must be wisdom in what He who brings it upon you, the Most Merciful, has caused to happen. Therefore we say: "I praise You, my Lord, for all Your judgment and all Your decree, a praise of contentment with Your rule, out of certainty in Your wisdom."

It is as if the Truth, may He be glorified, is saying to you: be mindful that not everything that you see as harmful according to your own laws is so; for the one who brings it upon you is the Most Merciful, and within the folds of this harm there is much benefit. Just as a tender father takes his son to the doctor, who performs a painful operation on him or removes a part of him to repair the rest of the body; this is harm in appearance, and in reality it is mercy towards him.

Therefore we have said before: if your son comes in bleeding, do not receive this except with contentment, not with anger, until you have asked about the one who did it. If he was an enemy, you may be angry with him; if he was a loving one, you accept what happened with contentment, and you say to the child: surely your uncle, for example, saw you making a mistake and punished you.

Likewise, do not judge God's decrees that He brings upon you except from the standpoint that they come from the Most Merciful, who is more merciful to you than a mother to her child, and you are His creation and His handiwork. We have never seen any of the foolish of mankind deliberately break his own handiwork; rather he takes care of it, and applies the hand of beautification and adornment to it, just as you see the carpenter, for example, holding the plane and carving the wood. Do you say he is harming his craft? No indeed, he is improving it and beautifying it.

Therefore the Most High says in the Hadith Qudsi: "After this affection of the Creator for the creation, would He bring upon them what harms them?"

In our practical life we often see examples of this matter. You often miss the train or the bus, for example, so you take the next appointment, and on the way you find that the train or bus has had an accident, so you correct your first notion yourself, and you turn your anger at missing the train into thanks to God who saved you, when you had thought otherwise. So: look to Him who brings the decrees upon you, and do not look to superficial benefit, for God, may He be exalted, has wisdom in what He brings about, whether you know it or do not know it.

Also, one of our children often fails an exam, for example, though he has studied, striven and acquired the sciences... etc., but some obstacle, such as an illness or other, came upon him and he was not granted success. The superficial view of things says: this is evil and loss that calls for anger, God forbid, but the patient and reflective view sees God's wisdom in this failure.

So the wise father in such situations says to his son: "O my son, praise God, for you are always successful, and perhaps if you succeed this year you will not be spared the eyes of the envious; and this is an opportunity for you to increase your total so that you may enter the college you want..." etc.

Thus the father strengthens his son's bond with God, increases his faith and his contentment with his Lord, and keeps him away from anger and from discontent with the decree, and this is a matter fathers should take care to attend to.

So: the point on which we wish to pause in this verse is that if the Most Merciful seems to you to contradict the act of harm, that is in your view, but for the one who brings it about there is no contradiction, because it is of the Most Merciful.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their intercession will not avail me anything﴾ [Yasin: 23], it means: the intercession of these gods, if they had any intercession, would be of no use, because they are associates of God and rivals to God, so how would their intercession be accepted by Him, glorified be He?

It is a condition of intercession that the intercessor be beloved to the one whose intercession is sought. These gods, even on the assumption that they had some intercession, would not be accepted by God, may He be exalted. Yet these gods in themselves are excused, since they have no sin; they did not claim to be gods, rather mankind claimed that.

We have previously mentioned that these gods disowned being worshipped besides God, and the poet who put this meaning into verse spoke truly, saying in the voice of these gods:

"They worshipped us, while we are more worshipful to God than those who stand in prayer at dawn;
they wronged, in ignorance, just as they wronged the son of Mary and his disciples;
they took our silence as evidence against us, so they became fuel for the Fire;
the extremist has his recompense, and the one exaggerated about returns to salvation by the mercy of the Forgiver."

As for His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿nor will they rescue me﴾ [Yasin: 23], because when an intercessor's intercession is rejected, he may be able to rescue the one interceded for from the hand of the one interceded with; but as for these gods, their intercession is not accepted, and they cannot rescue whoever asks them to intercede for him.

We have explained the meaning of intercession, that it comes from "shaf'" (pair): a person has a matter and cannot by himself resolve it by its causes, so he seeks help from another who supports him and joins him to strengthen him in resolving it. So: after he was alone, he becomes a pair with the intercessor, that is, two.

When the Truth, may He be glorified, wished to clarify this matter for us, He said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].

And He said in another place: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123].

You notice that the beginnings of the two verses agree but their endings differ, so why? They said: because the referent of the pronoun differs. Here there is a soul that recompenses and a soul that is recompensed for; if you return the pronoun to the one recompensed for, then the one recompensed for does not intercede for himself, rather he first offers ransom and seeks to make restitution for the harm in order to pay his ransom; if ransom is not accepted from him, he then looks for one who will intercede for him. So the meaning is: no ransom is accepted from the soul itself, and the intercession of others does not benefit it.

If you return the pronoun to the recompensing soul, that is, the interceding one, then the intercessor comes forward to intercede first; if his intercession is not accepted, he offers ransom and bears the ransom.

So: these gods, on the assumption that they have intercession, their intercession is rejected and unaccepted, and they also cannot rescue those who turn to them from the grip of the Truth, may He be glorified. They are not fit for intercession or for rescue, and this meaning is clear in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it; and if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj: 73].

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in clear error﴾ [Yasin: 24], it means: if I did that and went to worshipping these gods, I would be in clear ﴿error﴾ [Yasin: 24], evident and manifest. And His saying: ﴿in clear error﴾ [Yasin: 24] is as if error surrounds him and encompasses him from every side, such that he cannot escape from it.

Then this believing man says: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾ [Yasin: 25]. This address may be directed to the messengers whom the man came to support and assist in their call; so he looked at them and said: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord﴾ [Yasin: 25], and the meaning of ﴿so listen to me﴾ [Yasin: 25] is: listen to me as to what I give you in support, and bear witness for me that I volunteered this support of faith; no one assigned me to it.

It may also be that this address is directed to the disbelieving people, so he says to them: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord﴾ [Yasin: 25], meaning: God is your Lord in spite of you; and though you disbelieve in Him, may He be glorified, I have honored His lordship over you and believed in it, to enter into the greatness of this lordship. ﴿So listen to me﴾ [Yasin: 25]: listen to me in this proclamation, so that I may have fulfilled what was obligatory upon me toward you, and delivered the message to you without deceiving or cheating you.

Then the Truth, may He be glorified, says:

﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Would that my people knew..."﴾.

...among the qualifications of this man for entry into Paradise is that he did not look only to his own share of religious devotion; rather, he also looked to the share of his brethren. Even after he was given the glad tidings of Paradise, or after he had entered it, he was not preoccupied with its bliss to the exclusion of his people. Instead he said, ﴿Would that my people knew﴾, meaning: what I am in of bliss, and what the matter of faith and obedience has led to, so that they might act as I have acted and attain what I have attained. Indeed, had they known, they would have rushed toward faith and turned to obedience far more eagerly than they rush toward disbelief and sin.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 36, verse 27:

The construction of the verb (qīla, "it was said") in the passive voice conveys generality: who is the one who said to him, "Enter Paradise," and when did he say it? In the Qur'an there is a verse we read that answers this. Consider the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast — the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

So the man who took this stand of faith voluntarily, and who came from the farthest part of the city hastening to support the messengers in a matter he had not been charged with, and who came to the disbelieving people with proofs and evidences that the messengers themselves had not brought, is worthy that the angels descend upon him and that they give him good news of Paradise. Or: the Exalted has related what he says after he dies and enters Paradise, and this is an honouring from God for him.

Among the qualifications of this man for entry into Paradise is that he did not look only to his own share of devotion, but also looked to the share of his brethren. Even after he was given the good news of Paradise, or after he had entered it, he was not preoccupied with its bliss to the exclusion of his people; rather he said ﴿Would that my people knew﴾ [Ya-Sin: 26], meaning: what I am in of bliss, and what the matter of faith and obedience has come to, so that they might act as I have acted and attain what I have attained. Had they known, they would have rushed to faith and turned to obedience far more eagerly than they rush to disbelief and sin.

As for his saying ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured﴾ [Ya-Sin: 27], note that the forgiveness preceded the honour. This matter is called al-takhliyah wa-al-tahliyah (clearing away and adorning), and we have previously illustrated it with the garment when you wish to iron it, for example: do you take it to the presser (al-mukwaji) with the dirt still on it? No, you first clean it, and then you beautify it by ironing.

Likewise the Exalted — and to Allah belongs the highest likeness — before He admits His servant into Paradise, first purifies him of sins and cleanses him of what has clung to him; this is al-takhliyah. Then He honours him with Paradise; this is al-tahliyah. This meaning is clear in His saying: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has indeed succeeded﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185].

So the Exalted bestows His favour upon us first by drawing us away from the Fire through the forgiveness of sins, then He honours us with entry into Paradise as an honour and bounty from Him.

Then the Exalted says:

﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven, nor were We ever sending [it down].﴾…

We understand from the context of these two verses that the disbelieving people killed this volunteering man, or that he died naturally, and it is expected that God Most High would requite them for their denial of the three messengers first, and then for their denial of the man who came from the farthest part of the city striving to advise them. So what did God do to them?

He, glory be to Him, says: The matter of these deniers is too trivial for Us to send down upon them a host from the heaven to destroy them. A single cry is enough to destroy them. So the meaning of ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him﴾ [Yasin: 28], i.e., after the advice, the admonitions and the proofs that he volunteered with, ﴿any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down﴾ [Yasin: 28], meaning: We did not send down, and it was not fitting for Us to send down upon them a host from the heaven, because the matter is less than that.

﴿It was but one cry﴾ [Yasin: 29], i.e., there was only one cry, ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin: 29]. The word ﴿extinguished﴾ [Yasin: 29] indicates that they had been zealous in their disbelief in them, in fervour, rage and blazing against the messengers of God first, and then against the volunteering man second. They were in that like a blazing fire, and God extinguished it.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted, says after that a word which every believer may say when he sees the ends of the disobedient and the fate of the disbelievers whom death overtook before they could rescue themselves with faith. He says:

﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them...﴾.

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 36, verse 29:

﴿It was but a single shout, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾ That is: it was not but a single shout. ﴿Behold, they were extinguished.﴾ The word khamidun (extinguished) shows that they had been fervent in disbelief... in heat, anger and blazing against the messengers of God first, and then against the man who volunteered second. They were in that state like a blazing fire, and God extinguished them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 36, verse 30:

This is a word of regret, which we often say out of grief over the loss of good on the part of one for whom we wish good. The meaning of "yā ḥasratan" (﴿يٰحَسْرَةً﴾) here is a call, as if you were calling it: "O regret, come, for this is your time." The regret here is over the servants who denied the messengers of God and mocked them, and this is a matter over which every believer must feel regret, because God, Exalted, created you and provided for you before He summoned you into existence.

He created for you the means of your material life, and He preserved your body by what He decreed for you on earth of sustenance, necessities and luxuries. Is it conceivable that all of this be given to the body while the soul is left without giving, when the soul is more important than the body?

There must therefore be for the soul a giving, a nourishment and values. Indeed, values are what God requires of His servant, because you will be a worshipper of God, obedient to His commands, refraining from His prohibitions, and this is the method with which He charged you in "do such-and-such, and do not do such-and-such."

Therefore you find that the giving of matter and the means of sustaining the body is guaranteed to everyone: to the believer and the disbeliever, to the obedient and the disobedient, because God, Exalted, is the One who summoned all of them into existence; for this reason He undertook their provision, just as you, for example, invite a guest to your house and prepare for him his food, his drink and his lodging with you, and all people have received this giving.

As for the giving of values and the soul, some of them have received it and some have left it, because the giving of matter permitted him the desire of his self, whereas values restrained this desire and held it back from things his self wanted. So when values barred him from the desires of the self, he abandoned them and slipped away from them.

This value-based method came from one who loves you and is keen on your welfare...

So: every believer who sees the fate of the deniers and the downfall of the disbelievers in this story and in its like must say this word, "Oh, the regret over the servants!" Why? Because among the completeness of faith is that the believer grieves over one who has not tasted the sweetness of virtue and the pleasure of obedience; he is a pitiful one who deserves to be pitied and whose state one should lament. The believer loves for his brother what he loves for himself, and indeed loves good for all of humanity.

The commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 36, verse 31:

It means: it was enough for these deniers to look at the fate of those who denied before them, and at the punishment that befell them, and that after Allah destroyed them, none of them returned...

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. It means that among these people there were those who actually saw the places where the deniers met their end, and passed by their dwellings, which lie empty upon their roofs, during their journeys and trade caravans in winter and summer. The word kam (how many) indicates abundance, and that it is a matter beyond counting, just as you say to someone who denies your favour: "How much I have done good to you!" It is as though you are saying to him: "I accept your judgment, and I entrust you with the answer," and thereby your report is turned into an acknowledgment from him...

And His saying: ﴿that they do not return to them﴾ admits more than one meaning, according to the return of the pronoun in (annahum, "that they") and in (ilayhim, "to them"). The verse speaks of generations that were destroyed earlier and addresses contemporary deniers. If the pronoun of the third-person plural in (annahum) refers to the generations that were destroyed, then the meaning is: that they do not return, and we have not seen anyone of them return after his destruction. If the pronoun refers to the present addressees, then the meaning is: that you, the addressees, do not return in your lineage to those whom Allah destroyed, because Allah Most High uprooted them so that He left none of them, neither a person nor a descendant.

The verse, in its overall sense, means that the destruction of the disbelievers and deniers is no novelty; rather, it is a custom followed through the passage of time...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 36, verse 32:

That is: it was sufficient for these deniers to look at the fate of those who denied before them, and at the punishment that befell them, and that after God destroyed them not one of them returned. The word ﴿يَرَوْاْ﴾ [Yasin: 31] comes from the verb ra'a (to see), and it comes in two senses: visual (basariyya) or cognitive (ilmiyya). You say "I saw the scene" (ra'aytu al-mashhad), and this is visual seeing; and you say "I saw this opinion" (ra'aytu hadha al-ra'y), meaning "I knew it." Visual seeing limits your knowledge to what your organ of sense has reached, whereas cognitive seeing gives you what your organ of sense and the organs of others have reached. Cognitive seeing, then, is broader than visual seeing.

Therefore God, the Exalted, said, addressing His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [Al-Fil: 1].

It is well known that the Messenger of God ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, and perhaps after this event; so he did not witness any of it with visual sight, yet his Lord addressed him with "Have you not considered" [Al-Fil: 1], meaning "Did you not know," whether his people had related the story to him or God the Exalted had informed him of it.

Visual witnessing of events is the most reliable means of perception, for, as they say, "there is no 'where' with the eye" (laysa ma'a al-ayn ayn). But why did the context shift from "Did you not know" to "Did you not see"? They said: in this there is an indication from the Truth, glorified is He, to His Prophet, saying to him: My informing you of a matter of knowledge is more reliable than your seeing it with your own eye.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did they not see﴾ [Yasin: 31], it means that among these people were those who in fact saw the sites of the deniers' destruction, and passed by their dwellings which were lying in ruins, on their journeys and trading trips in winter and summer. The word ﴿كَمْ﴾ [Yasin: 31] indicates multitude, and that it is a matter beyond counting, just as you say to someone who denies your favour: "How much I have done good to you!", as if you are saying to him: I accept your judgment and entrust you with the answer; and thereby your statement turns from an assertion of yours into an acknowledgment from him.

The meaning of ﴿مِّنَ ٱلْقُرُونِ﴾ [Yasin: 31]: qurun is the plural of qarn, which is a period of time that they estimated at a hundred years. Qarn also means a group or people united by one thing, however long its period, such as one religion, or the rule of one king, etc. For example, we say "the people of Noah," who took a span of a thousand years or more.

As for His saying: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ [Yasin: 31], it admits more than one meaning according to what the pronoun in (annahum) and in (ilayhim) refers back to. The verse speaks of generations destroyed before and addresses contemporary deniers. If the pronoun of the absent ones in (annahum) refers to the generations that were destroyed, then the meaning is: they do not return, and we have not seen any one of them return after his destruction. If the pronoun refers to the present addressees, then the meaning is: you, the addressees, do not return in your lineage to these whom God destroyed, because God the Exalted uprooted them so that He left none of them, neither any offspring.

The verse as a whole means that the destruction of the disbelievers and deniers is no novelty; rather it is a custom followed through the passage of time. The Qur'an relates to us what befell ʿAd, Thamud and Pharaoh: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿAd, Iram of the pillars, the like of which was not created in the lands, and Thamud who hewed the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh of the stakes, who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein?﴾ [Al-Fajr: 6-12].

God the Exalted has left the traces to show us the truth of what He, glorified is He, has informed us. And here we see America, for example, the mistress of modern civilization, possessor of precedence in innovation, invention and the conquest of space; yet they come to Egypt to view the monuments of the Pharaohs, which were built thousands of years before the Christian era, and they marvel, despite their scientific advancement, at how the pyramids were built, for example.

This custom, the custom of the destruction of the disbelievers, we see its witnesses in our modern age. Russia, which committed suicide and killed itself by its own hand — look at what it did in Chechnya, this small Islamic state, while we fell short in supporting them, or our support was not commensurate with the might of the aggressors; therefore heaven intervened, and God repelled the enemies of His religion and avenged Himself on them in the earthquake of Sakhalin.

As for His saying, in the verse after it: ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us, present﴾ [Yasin: 32], this verse came after His saying ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ [Yasin: 31] to clarify that the non-return is in this world; for if they had no return either in this world or the Hereafter, then death would be a rest for these deniers. As al-Fakhr al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, said, the intended meaning is: they do not return in this world, but in the Hereafter there must be a return for reckoning concerning every great and small deed.

His saying, glorified is He, (wa-in): here in means the negating ma (mā al-nāfiya), and (lamma) means "except" (illa). So the meaning is: "And not all of them except as a gathered whole brought before Us." We have known from our study of the rules of grammar that kull and jamī' are words of moral emphasis for the plural, and likewise abṣaʿ, akta' and abta' (ʿ-forms of emphasis), as you say: "The people came, all of them (ajmaʿūn), or (abṣaʿūn) or (abtaʿūn)," and "The people came, all of them (kulluhum)." We observe that the verse combined the two emphatic words kull and jamī', so why?

They said: the combination of the two here is necessary, because each of them has a meaning that the other does not convey. The totality (kulliyya) indicates inclusiveness of the individuals in the return, so kulluhum means every single one of them, and it is not required that they be gathered together; rather each comes alone, so that the humiliation and lowliness of the extravagant and of the disbelievers who made themselves worshipped gods may be seen. As for jamī', it means: they come gathered together.

The meaning of ﴿مُحْضَرُونَ﴾ [Yasin: 32] is from the verb ḥaḍara, and there is a difference between ḥaḍara and uḥḍira. Ḥaḍara means he came of his own accord and by his own will; whereas uḥḍira means he was compelled to attend, forced against his will.

After the Exalted mentioned the question of resurrection in ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us, present﴾ [Yasin: 32], He, glorified is He, wished to mention a proof of the truth of this matter, because resurrection is among the matters that many deny, and the poet spoke truly:

The astrologer and the physician both claim that bodies are not gathered; I say to you both:
If your words are true, I am not a loser; but if my words are true, the loss is upon you both.

And as a sincere adviser says to you: if you go along such-and-such a road, beware and take precaution, for there are wolves, beasts and highwaymen in it; what harm is there to you if you took precaution and found nothing of what frightened you? Likewise, my belief in resurrection, if it does not benefit me, does not harm me; and your belief, if it does not harm you, does not benefit you.

The strongest objection regarding the resurrection of bodies among the philosophers is that they said: suppose a man died and was buried, and his body decomposed, and a tree was planted on his grave which was nourished from his remains, then it bore fruit, and another man ate of its fruit; so elements of the first reached the second. When resurrection comes, to whom will these elements be resurrected: to the first, or to the second?

The proponent of this objection understood that elements, when they form, have a particularity in composition, and did not understand that they have a generality of kind in aggregation. How? We say: suppose a man was afflicted with an illness that reduced his weight by twenty kilos, for example, then God guided the physician to his ailment, and he prescribed the medicine, and he was healed from his illness and was nourished until he returned to his former weight. Where did the elements that had been lost from him go, and is it the very same quantity of elements that returned to him after he was healed?

Thus: the matter is not a particularity of elements, but a quantity of elements; and the greatness lies in our counting the quantity of elements of each person. In another place, the Truth, glorified is He, responds to the deniers of resurrection, saying to them: why do you obstinately deny resurrection, when it is the restoration of something that existed already and whose elements were scattered? And what is more amazing is that He originated it from non-existence; so resurrection is easier than origination: ﴿And He it is who originates creation then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [Al-Rum: 27]. This is if we go along with you in your understanding of matters and follow your laws of thinking.

It has already been explained that the elements which God created in the cosmos are the same, having neither increased nor decreased. Water, for example, is the very same water since God created the earth, but it circulates in a known cycle: a man, for example, drinks many tons of water throughout his life; does he retain it? No, rather it leaves him in the form of urine and the like, and even after he dies, the water within him evaporates, and the earth absorbs it to begin a new cycle of water. Likewise the elements of man go through this cycle.

﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth: We have revived it and brought forth from it grain...﴾.

This is a proof visible to all, and no one can deny it. We see the dead, barren, parched earth, and when the rain comes it turns green, life stirs in it, it quivers and swells. A person should take from what he observes a proof of the truth of what is beyond his observation.

This verse may be taken either as a cosmic sign that points to the power of the Originator, glory be to Him, or as a proof that when We send down rain upon the dead earth, it quivers and brings forth every lovely pair.

It suffices that it is our resting place: upon it we settle, and to it we return. How much more, then, when God grants it a measure of life, as it quivers with vegetation and turns into a wonderful green.

The revival of the earth comes in degrees. Either it is revived with plants that do not sustain food, such as grass, herbs and turf, and it suffices that this kind clothes the face of the earth in beauty and freshness, binds the sand and fixes it on the surface of the earth so that the winds do not scatter it into our eyes. It is therefore a manifestation of the earth's life and one of God's blessings. The other degree is that the earth brings forth the plants by which we sustain ourselves, and these are of two kinds: grains, which represent the essentials and are among the foundations of your life and the root of sustenance, the most important of which is wheat.

This was the food of the elite and the wealthy, until we became alert to the importance of bran, so that we came to prefer it over fine flour. The evidence is that bread made from bran is now more expensive than white bread. For this reason it is narrated that our master Sulayman, peace be upon him, to whom God had given a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, used to eat only the khushkar, that is, the coarse flour, while the fine flour ('alama) was for the servants.

Then there are fruits, which are counted among the luxuries we enjoy.

"The food of the poor and the sweet of the rich, and the provision of the traveler and the expatriate."

Everything in it is beneficial and useful. It suffices that you know that nothing of the palm tree is ever thrown away, and every part of it has a use and a function: the trunk, the fronds, and the fibers.
